docs.title: Flow Unofficial Documentation
docs.text:
Flow is an experimental layout manager and formspec API replacement for Luanti (formerly Minetest). Describe your menu, and flow handles the rest. Vaguely inspired by Flutter and GTK.

Luanti's built-in menu format (inventories, chests, dialogs, ...) is formspec, consisting of one long string of buttons, text fields, and inventory slots. With formspec, you have to manually place every element by position and size, consult official docs in case of the many gotchas, and there's no reasonable way to write an LSP for it.

Flow lets you describe the same menu with plain Lua tables, positions and sizes everything for you, and generates the formspec behind the scenes. You never have to write one. And if you like using modern IDE features, you will now actually have direct access to definitions from the editor (LuaCATS annotations are included).

Online tutorial/demo (source)

docs.title: Terms Used in This Documentation
docs.text: Term Meaning Form A menu made with flow, created with flow.make_gui() and shown with form:show(). This documentation does not call it a "gui". Formspec Luanti's own text format for menus. Flow generates formspecs for you. Element One part of a form, such as a label, a button, or a box. Elements are made with the functions in flow.widgets (the name of that table is the only place "widget" is used). Build function The function you pass to flow.make_gui(). It returns the elements of the form and is called every time the form is drawn. Root element The element that the build function returns, which holds everything else in the form. Container An element that holds other elements. gui.Container is the one whose elements you place yourself with x and y. Layout element An element that arranges the elements inside it, such as gui.VBox, gui.HBox, and gui.Stack, see Layout Elements. Flow The mod. gui.Flow (written with the gui. prefix) is an element of the mod that wraps its children onto new rows. ctx The context table of a form, see Getting Started.

docs.title: Layouting
docs.text:
• Automatic placement. Flow works out every position, so there's no arithmetic to redo when you add one button.
  • Comprehensive layout elements. Nest HBox and VBox containers and they line up on their own. Scrolling, paging, stacking, wrapping, and flexible spacing are covered too. And yes, also manual placement using Container.
  • Automatic sizing. Labels, checkboxes, buttons, text fields, password fields, text areas, drop-downs, text lists, and vertical labels size themselves. See Sizes.
  • Room to grow. Set expand = true and an element fills any spare space.
  • Translation-friendly. Elements sized from their label grow or shrink to fit longer text1.

docs.title: Other Features
docs.text:
• No form names. They still exist internally, but you never have to deal with them.
  • No state bookkeeping. Flow remembers the values of fields, scrollbars, checkboxes, and the like across redraws, and reapplies them for you.
  • Built-in debugging. The inspector mod helps you develop and debug forms.
  • Safer input handling. Flow mitigates some common formspec input security issues. See Security.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: • This mod doesn't support all of the features that regular formspecs do. See Unsupported Features for a list.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Flow ignores potentially malicious formspec input from clients, such as buttons or fields that haven't been shown to the client, out-of-bounds dropdown selections, and newlines in Field elements (where it's impossible to enter a newline without pasting it in). See Security for the full list of what flow checks and what you still need to check yourself.

docs.title: Other Documentation
docs.text:
The official documentation is available at https://luk3yx.gitlab.io/minetest-flow/. Some code snippets have a "run" button which will open them in a web-based playground, not all of these will work properly as the playground doesn't support all formspec elements.

  1. This is an estimate, not a measurement. The real size of a label depends on the client's font, DPI, window size, and formspec scaling settings, and Luanti gives mods no way to measure text. Flow assumes 0.21 slots per character (UTF-8 characters, not bytes, counting the longest line) and 0.4 slots per line of height, scaled by any *1.5-style font_size style. It ignores the font. If the estimate is off for your text, set w, h, or min_w yourself. ↩

docs.title: Common Aspects
docs.text:
All flow elements (widgets) draw something, change size/position of other elements, or accept input. Every element is a function in flow.widgets that takes a table of parameters. For example:

local gui = flow.widgets

gui.Label { label = "Hello world!" }

docs.title: Sizes
docs.text:
Sizes are measured in inventory slots: 1 is the width and height of one item slot. There is no hidden padding or spacing, so two boxes that are 1 wide and placed next to each other with spacing = 0 touch. You never give an element a position, boxes place their children and flow works out the total size of the form.

Elements that show text, such as labels, buttons, and fields, are sized to fit their text unless you give them a w and h. Elements that show something without a natural size, such as images, boxes, models, and tables, need an explicit w and h (their parameter lists below do not say -- Optional). Flow can only estimate the width of text because the real width depends on the player's font, screen size, and scaling settings, so avoid layouts that rely on exact text widths (see the note on label sizes).

docs.title: Which Elements Take w, h, min_w, and min_h
docs.text:
Elements that size themselves are the ones flow can work out a size for: from their text (labels, buttons, fields, dropdowns, text lists), or from the elements inside them (containers and boxes). For these, w and h are optional, and min_w and min_h set a lower limit on the size flow works out. min_w and min_h only apply to a dimension that flow works out itself: if you set both w and h, both minimums are ignored, and if you set only w, min_w is ignored and min_h still applies. Elements that cannot size themselves ignore min_w and min_h.

Element w and h min_w and min_h gui.Label Optional Yes gui.Vertlabel, gui.Checkbox Not supported, always sized automatically Yes gui.Button, gui.ButtonExit, gui.ButtonURL Optional Yes gui.ImageButton, gui.ImageButtonExit, gui.ItemImageButton Optional, the size is worked out from the label like a button (at least 1.6 by 0.8), so you usually want to set them Yes gui.ButtonUrlExit Required, it has no automatic size (see the note below the table) No gui.Field, gui.Pwdfield, gui.Textarea, gui.Dropdown, gui.Textlist Optional Yes gui.Container, gui.ScrollContainer Optional, the size is worked out from the elements inside Yes gui.HBox, gui.VBox, gui.Stack Not supported, use min_w and min_h. The exception is a gui.Stack with both set, for manual positioning, see the warning in Layout Elements Yes gui.ScrollableVBox, gui.PaginatedVBox Optional Not checked gui.Spacer Optional Not checked gui.Flow w required, h not supported No gui.Image, gui.AnimatedImage, gui.ItemImage, gui.Model Required No gui.Box, gui.Table, gui.Hypertext, gui.Scrollbar, gui.Tabheader Required No gui.List Required, in slots rather than in size units No gui.Background, gui.Background9 Required, unless auto_clip is true No

An element without a size that needs one is written to the form with an empty size, which Luanti rejects, so you will see it as a broken form rather than an error message. gui.ButtonUrlExit has no automatic size, unlike gui.ButtonURL, so its w and h are required, see gui.ButtonUrlExit.

docs.title: Names and Values
docs.text:
Many elements take a name. Input elements (fields, checkboxes, dropdowns, lists of text, tables, ...) with a name have their current value stored in ctx.form[name] and flow remembers it when the form is redrawn:

Element Value in ctx.form[name] gui.Field, gui.Pwdfield, gui.Textarea Text (string) gui.Checkbox true or false gui.Dropdown Text of the selected item, or its number if index_event = true gui.Textlist, gui.Table Number of the selected row (first row is 1) gui.Tabheader Number of the selected tab (first tab is 1) gui.Scrollbar Position of the slider (number) gui.Hypertext "action:" and the name of the last clicked <action> link

Until the player changes something, the value is the element's initial value (default, selected, selected_idx, value, current_tab). If you did not give one, it is "" for text, false for checkboxes, 1 for tables, text lists, and dropdowns with index_event = true, the text of the first item for other dropdowns, and 0 for scrollbars. gui.Hypertext has no starting value, and neither has gui.Tabheader without a current_tab, so ctx.form[name] is nil until the player clicks a link or a tab. Text fields only send their text to the server when the player presses a button or Enter, so ctx.form can be out of date until then.

If your build function reads ctx.form.some_name, flow redraws the form automatically whenever the player changes that value (unless the element has its own on_event), see Redrawing When a Value Changes. Buttons do not store a value.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Elements that the player can use accept an on_event function, which is called with the player and ctx. Return true from it to redraw the form. A name is optional if you use on_event, flow makes one up.

Flow has four callbacks. All of them are called with the player and ctx:

Callback Put it on Called when Return true on_event Any element the player can use The client sends the element's name: a button when it is clicked, an input when the player changes it. A text field is sent with every submission, so its on_event is called whenever the player presses any button or Enter. Redraws the form. on_key_enter, see Handling Enter Keypresses in Fields gui.Field, gui.Pwdfield The player presses Enter in the field. The on_event of the same field is called as well. Redraws the form. on_quit, see Running Code When a Form Is Closed gui.Container, gui.HBox, gui.VBox, gui.Stack The client closes the form. Return nothing. on_close_popover, see Popovers The container that has a popover The player clicks outside the popover. Redraws the form.

Only one button callback runs for each submission, and it runs after all other callbacks, see Security. This includes on_close_popover, which flow handles as a button. on_event on a text field is easy to mix up with on_key_enter: on_event is called on any submission, on_key_enter only when Enter is pressed.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text:
Colors are strings. "#RGB" and "#RRGGBB" are fully opaque, while "#RGBA" and "#RRGGBBAA" end with an alpha value, where 00 is fully transparent and FF is fully opaque. Color names also work (all the names from CSS, such as "red" and "darkgreen"), and you can add an alpha value after a # to a color name. The alpha value is one or two hexadecimal digits, so "darkgreen#08" is dark green with an alpha of 08 (hex, about 3% opaque) and "darkgreen#80" is about half transparent.

Warning: gui.Box, and the bgcolor of containers (which flow draws with a box), are the exception to the opaque rule: a "#RGB" or "#RRGGBB" color there is drawn semitransparent. Color names are not affected. See gui.Box.

Most text can also be coloured by putting color escape sequences in it, such as the ones made by core.colorize(). Dropdown items and tab captions are an exception, they cannot be coloured.

docs.title: Textures and Items
docs.text: A texture name is the file name of an image from the textures folder of any loaded mod, such as "default_dirt.png". An item name is the registered name of an item or node, such as "unifieddyes:colorium".

docs.title: Invisible Elements
docs.text:
Some elements draw nothing and take up no space in a gui.HBox, gui.VBox, or gui.Stack. They change how a nearby element looks or behaves, and where you put them matters:

Element Where it goes What it affects gui.Style Before The element with that name gui.StyleType Before Every element of that type after it gui.SetFocus Before The element with that name gui.Listcolors Before The gui.List elements after it gui.TableColumns Before The gui.Table after it gui.TableOptions Before The gui.Table after it gui.ScrollbarOptions Before The gui.Scrollbar elements after it gui.Tooltip After The element with the name in gui_element_name gui.Listring After The gui.List elements it names, or the last two lists before it if it has no parameters

The style and tooltip parameters that every element has are the exception: flow inserts the matching style or tooltip element directly before the element for you, so you do not need to place anything, see Styling and Tooltips. The "before" rule for the others comes from Luanti, and so does the "after" rule of gui.Tooltip. An invisible element is skipped when flow works out sizes and spacing, so putting one between two elements does not add a gap. gui.Nil is one as well: it is a tooltip that is hidden, which is why it takes no space.

docs.title: Parameters Shared by All Elements
docs.text:
Every element, including Layout Elements, accepts these parameters in addition to its own:

Parameter Description padding Space around the element, see Padding. visible Set to false to hide the element but keep its space, see Hiding Elements. expand Set to true to make the element grow to fill spare space in the gui.HBox or gui.VBox it is in. If several elements expand, they share the spare space equally. align_h, align_v Where the element goes when there is more room than it needs: "start", "end", "center", "fill" (stretch), or "auto" (the default, flow picks one). "left" and "top" mean "start", "right" and "bottom" mean "end", and "center" means "center". min_w, min_h The smallest size of the element, for elements that size themselves, see Which Elements Take w, h, min_w, and min_h. tooltip Text to show when the player hovers over the element, see Tooltips. style Inline styles, see Styling. on_event A function to call when the player uses the element, see Events above.

docs.title: Automatic Alignment
docs.text:
"auto" only matters when an element is given more room than it needs. That happens across a box (the width in a gui.VBox, the height in a gui.HBox), along a box for elements with expand = true, and for every element in a gui.Stack. Flow then picks by the type of the element:

Element What "auto" does gui.Image, gui.AnimatedImage, gui.Model, gui.ItemImageButton Centered. gui.List Centered (a list cannot be stretched). gui.Label (vertically) Centered in the spare height. gui.Label (horizontally) Stays at the start, unless it has expand = true and the spare room is along the box. It is then stretched, which centers the text (see the centering hack in gui.Spacer). gui.Checkbox Centered vertically. Horizontally it stays at the start, unless it has expand = true and the spare room is along the box, then it is centered. Everything else (buttons, fields, boxes, containers, ...) Stretched to fill the spare room.

Set align_h or align_v yourself to override this. Which elements need a w and h, and which do not, is a separate question, see Sizes above.

docs.title: Nine-Slice Images
docs.text:
Images and image-like backgrounds can optionally be drawn as a "nine-slice". The picture is cut into a 3x3 grid, where the corners keep their size, the edges are stretched in one direction, and the middle is stretched in both. This lets one small texture make a panel or border of any size without distorting its corners. The middle_* parameters describe where the cuts are, in texture pixels (whole numbers):

  • middle_x only: the cuts are middle_x pixels from every side.
  • middle_x and middle_y: middle_x pixels from the left and right sides and middle_y pixels from the top and bottom.
  • All four: the middle rectangle starts at middle_x, middle_y and ends at middle_x2, middle_y2. Negative middle_x2 and middle_y2 values are measured from the far (right/bottom) edge of the texture.

Here is the grid. The two vertical cuts are at x and x2, and the two horizontal cuts are at y and y2 (the names are those of the middle_* parameters):

      x                x2
      |                |
  +---+----------------+---+
  | 1 |       2        | 3 |  <- above y
y-+---+----------------+---+
  | 4 |       5        | 6 |
  |   |                |   |
  +---+----------------+---+
y2| 7 |       8        | 9 |  <- below y2
  +---+----------------+---+

Parts 1, 3, 7, and 9 (the corners) keep their size. Parts 2 and 8 are stretched sideways, parts 4 and 6 are stretched up and down, and part 5 is stretched in both directions.

docs.title: Nine-Slice Formats
docs.text:
The same cuts are written in three ways, depending on where they are used:

Where Parameter How it is written Meaning Elements with middle_* parameters, such as gui.Background9 and gui.AnimatedImage middle_x, middle_y, middle_x2, middle_y2 Separate numbers As described above. bgimg_middle on the root element or a box or container, see Padding bgimg_middle One number Same as middle_x alone: that many pixels from every side. bgimg_middle and fgimg_middle in a button style bgimg_middle, fgimg_middle A string: "x", "x,y", or "x,y,x2,y2" The same as middle_x; middle_x and middle_y; or all four.

docs.title: Experimental Features
docs.text: These features might be broken in the future. Popovers are also experimental, and have their own page.

docs.title: no_prepend
docs.text:
Games and mods can add extra content to the start of every form shown to a player with player:set_formspec_prepend(), for example to give all forms the same background or style. This is called a "prepend", and it can be why a form has a background or style you did not expect.

You can set no_prepend = true on the "root" element to stop prepends from being applied to a form.

To see what no_prepend does, this example gives the player a prepend that makes every button red. Tick the checkbox and the red disappears:

local gui = flow.widgets
local player = core.get_player_by_name("current_player")

-- Make every button red, like a game's prepend could.
player:set_formspec_prepend("style_type[button;bgcolor=red]")

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        -- Ignore the prepend while the box is ticked.
        no_prepend = ctx.form.skip or false,

        gui.Checkbox { name = "skip", label = "Set no_prepend" },
        gui.Button { label = "Am I red?" },
    }
end)

form:show(player)

docs.title: bgcolor
docs.text:
You can set bgcolor = "#123", fbgcolor = "#123", and bg_fullscreen = true on the root element to set background colors:

  • bgcolor: The color of the background of the form itself.
  • fbgcolor: The color of the fullscreen background, which covers the whole screen behind the form.
  • bg_fullscreen: Which of the two colors to draw, see the table below.

The value of bg_fullscreen decides what is drawn. true can look backwards: it does not add the fullscreen background to the form's own one, it switches to the fullscreen one.

bg_fullscreen bgcolor (the form) fbgcolor (the screen) false (the default) drawn not drawn true not drawn drawn "both" drawn drawn "neither" not drawn not drawn

Flow passes these three values straight to Luanti's bgcolor[] formspec element, so Luanti decides what is drawn. This also means that fbgcolor is not drawn unless you set bg_fullscreen to true or "both".

Colors that you leave out are not changed. See Common Aspects for how colors are written.

gui.VBox {
    -- Draw a blue form on a dimmed screen
    bgcolor = "#336699",
    fbgcolor = "#00000080",
    bg_fullscreen = "both",
    gui.Label { label = "Hello world!" },
}

docs.title: Window Position
docs.text:
These values allow the position of the displayed form to be moved around and adjust how it is scaled. You will likely need them for most HUDs, which are described in Using a Form as a HUD.

Example:

local my_gui = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        -- The point on the screen where the form is placed, and the point
        -- on the form that goes there. 0 is top/left, 1 is bottom/right,
        -- and the default is {x = 0.5, y = 0.5} (center). You usually want
        -- both to be the same. This is the bottom-right corner.
        window_position = { x = 1, y = 1 },
        window_anchor = { x = 1, y = 1 },

        -- Minimum space around the form as a fraction of the screen (here
        -- 10% left/right and 20% top/bottom). Too-big forms are scaled
        -- down, and negative values let the form go off the edge.
        -- Default for forms: {x = 0.05, y = 0.05}. HUDs default to a
        -- hardcoded pixel size.
        window_padding = { x = 0.1, y = 0.2 },

        gui.Label { label = "Hello world" },
    }
end)

docs.title: Rendering to a Formspec
docs.text:
This API should only be used when necessary and may have breaking changes in the future.

Luanti describes menus with formspec strings (see the introduction), which flow normally generates and shows for you. Some APIs in other mods, such as sfinv (see Using a Form as an Inventory), expect formspec strings instead. You can use this API to embed flow forms inside them. To use flow with these mods, you can call form:render_to_formspec_string(player, ctx, standalone).

  • A complete formspec starts with a formspec_version[] element (the version of the formspec language it uses) and a size[] element (the size of the form). By default these aren't included in the returned formspec, and are returned in a third value instead: a table info with w and h (the size of the form, in the units described in Sizes) and formspec_version (the version number). Set standalone to include them in the returned formspec string. The third return value will not be returned (it is nil).
  • Returns formspec, process_event[, info], see the two forms below. info.formspec_version is always 7, whatever the player's client supports. Pass the same ctx again when you redraw so the form keeps its values.
  • Call process_event(fields) with the fields table that Luanti passes to core.register_on_player_receive_fields callbacks. It returns true if the formspec should be redrawn, where render_to_formspec_string should be called and the new process_event should be used in the future. It returns true when an on_event or on_key_enter function returned true, or when the player changed a value that the build function read from ctx.form. This is also the case when fields.quit is set (for example when the player clicks a gui.ButtonExit whose on_event returns true), because flow does not look at fields.quit itself. The form is closing then, so callers normally skip the redraw, as the example below does.

The two call forms side by side:

-- Embeddable: size and version come back as a third value.
local fs, process_event, info =
    form:render_to_formspec_string(player, ctx)
-- info.w, info.h and info.formspec_version (always 7) are set.

-- Standalone: fs starts with formspec_version[] and size[], and there is
-- no third value.
local fs, process_event =
    form:render_to_formspec_string(player, ctx, true)

Here is a complete example. It wraps a flow form in a formspec of its own and shows it with core.show_formspec. The label above the form belongs to the outer formspec, and the counter keeps working because process_event handles the button click:

local gui = flow.widgets

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Label { label = "I am a flow form inside a formspec!" },
        gui.Label { label = "Clicks: " .. (ctx.clicks or 0) },
        gui.Button {
            label = "Click me",
            on_event = function(player, ctx)
                ctx.clicks = (ctx.clicks or 0) + 1
                return true
            end,
        },
    }
end)

local FORMNAME = "mymod:outer"
local contexts = {}
local handlers = {}

local function show(player)
    local name = player:get_player_name()
    contexts[name] = contexts[name] or {}

    -- Pass the same ctx every time so values survive redraws.
    local fs, process_event, info =
        form:render_to_formspec_string(player, contexts[name])
    handlers[name] = process_event

    -- Put the generated elements inside a formspec of our own.
    core.show_formspec(name, FORMNAME, table.concat({
        ("formspec_version[%d]"):format(info.formspec_version),
        ("size[%f,%f]"):format(info.w + 2, info.h + 3),
        "label[1,0.7;This label belongs to the outer formspec]",
        "container[1,1.5]", fs, "container_end[]",
    }))
end

core.register_on_player_receive_fields(function(player, formname, fields)
    if formname ~= FORMNAME then return end

    -- Redraw when flow asks for it.
    local process_event = handlers[player:get_player_name()]
    if process_event and process_event(fields) and not fields.quit then
        show(player)
    end
end)

show(core.get_player_by_name("current_player"))

Warning: Do not use this API with node meta formspecs (formspecs that are stored in the metadata of a node), it can and will break!

docs.title: Embedding a Form Into Another Form
docs.text:
You can embed form objects inside others like this:

local gui = flow.widgets

local other_form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.Label { label = "I am embedded" }
end)

local parent_form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Label { label = "Hello world" },
        other_form:embed {
            -- A name for the embed, see below.
            name = "my_embed_name",
        },
    }
end)

Current versions of flow ignore a player parameter in the table passed to embed. Versions from before 2025-06-17 need player = player, so add it if your mod has to work with them.

Special characters (excluding - and _) are not allowed in embed names.

The name changes a lot about how the embedded form works:

With name Without name ctx in the embedded form Its own table, at ctx.my_embed_name in the parent's ctx The same ctx as the parent ctx.form in the embedded form Reads and writes go to the parent's ctx.form, with the field names rewritten (the name of the embed is added to the start) The same ctx.form as the parent Field names, scrollbar names, tooltip names, and style selectors Rewritten, so they cannot clash with the parent's Not rewritten, so a name used in both forms is the same input on_event, on_quit, and on_close_popover functions Called with the embedded form's own ctx Called with the shared ctx on_key_enter functions Called with the parent's ctx, not the embedded form's (a known limitation, see below) Called with the shared ctx

Events and redraws work through the parent. The embedded form's elements are part of the parent's form, so a callback that returns true redraws the whole parent form, and update and update_where called on the embedded form object do nothing, because the form that is open belongs to the parent. Call them on the parent form object instead.

Known limitation: the on_key_enter function of a field in a form embedded with a name is called with the parent's ctx, unlike on_event, which gets the embedded form's own ctx. In that function ctx.form.my_field is nil, because the value is stored under the rewritten field name, and anything you store in ctx goes into the parent's ctx. To reach the embedded form's own ctx from there, go through the embed's entry in the parent's ctx, for example ctx.my_embed_name.form.my_field. Embeds without a name are not affected, because they share the parent's ctx anyway.

docs.title: Running Code When a Form Is Closed
docs.text:
gui.Container, gui.HBox, gui.VBox, and gui.Stack elements support an on_quit callback which gets run when a player closes a form (for example by pressing Escape or clicking an exit button).

Note that this function is not called in some cases, such as when the player leaves without closing the form or when another form/formspec is shown.

This function must not return anything, behaviour may get added to return values in the future.

local gui = flow.widgets

-- A second form that pops up once the first one is closed.
local closed_notice = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Label { label = "Form closed!" },
        gui.ButtonExit { label = "OK" },
    }
end)

local my_gui = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        on_quit = function(player, ctx)
            core.chat_send_player(player:get_player_name(), "Form closed!")

            -- Defer so the new form is not closed along with this one.
            core.after(0, function()
                closed_notice:show(player)
            end)
        end,

        gui.Label { label = "Press Escape or the button to close me." },
        gui.ButtonExit { label = "Close" },
    }
end)

my_gui:show(core.get_player_by_name("current_player"))

If multiple on_quit callbacks are specified in different elements, they will all get called.

docs.title: Handling Enter Keypresses in Fields
docs.text:
Several options deal with the Enter key:

  • on_key_enter is called when the player presses Enter in a gui.Field or gui.Pwdfield.
  • on_event on the same field is called whenever the client submits the field, which includes Enter but is not limited to it. Be careful not to use it by mistake.
  • close_on_enter makes Enter close the form (gui.Field only). It is the same as gui.FieldCloseOnEnter. Without an on_key_enter callback flow logs a warning, because closing is the only thing Enter would do.
  • enter_after_edit makes Android's "Done" button count as Enter (experimental). It is the same as gui.FieldEnterAfterEdit.

Also provide another way to trigger the action, such as a button, in case this API is replaced.

gui.Field and gui.Pwdfield support an on_key_enter callback that gets called if enter is pressed:

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Field {
            label = "Press enter!",
            name = "field",
            on_key_enter = function(player, ctx)
                core.chat_send_player(player:get_player_name(),
                    "Field value: " .. dump(ctx.form.field))

                -- Show the result in the form as well.
                ctx.enters = (ctx.enters or 0) + 1
                ctx.last_value = ctx.form.field
                return true
            end,

            -- Pressing enter does not close the form by default. You can
            -- specify close_on_enter to close it when enter is pressed.
            -- This only applies to gui.Field.
            close_on_enter = ctx.form.close or false,
        },
        gui.Checkbox { name = "close", label = "Close the form on enter" },
        gui.Label {
            label = ("Enter pressed %d times, last value: %s"):format(
                ctx.enters or 0, dump(ctx.last_value)),
        },
    }
end)

Press enter and the label counts the key presses. If you tick the checkbox first, enter closes the form as well.

docs.title: Getting a Reference to the Current Player and Context
docs.text:
If you're making a custom element, it might be useful to get a reference to ctx and player so you don't have to pass them in manually.

local function HelloWorld(def)
    local ctx, player = flow.get_context()
    return gui.Label {
        label = "Hello, " .. player:get_player_name() .. "!\n" ..
            "some_value=" .. ctx.some_value,
        style = def.style,
    }
end

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    ctx.some_value = 123
    return HelloWorld { style = { font_size = "*2" } }
end)

flow.get_context() will error when called outside a build function (as you should not normally do this).

docs.title: gui.Flow Container
docs.text:
gui.Flow is a fixed-width container that wraps items around if they don't fit. Unlike other elements, you must specify a width, and some options like min_w and padding aren't supported.

This is similar to GTK's FlowBox, but with a lot fewer features.

The width also has to leave room for the spacing between elements. spacing has the same default as for gui.VBox (0.2, see also Padding). Flow needs w to be at least 1 + 0.2 + 1 + 0.2 + 1 (3.4) to fit three 1-wide elements on one row, and at least 4.6 to fit four, so 3 * (1 + 0.2) (3.6) is a safe width for three.

gui.Flow {
    -- Fits 3 items, including the default spacing
    w = 3 * (1 + 0.2),

    -- Five colored squares: three on the first row, two on the second.
    gui.Box { w = 1, h = 1, color = "#E74C3C" },
    gui.Box { w = 1, h = 1, color = "#E67E22" },
    gui.Box { w = 1, h = 1, color = "#F1C40F" },
    gui.Box { w = 1, h = 1, color = "#2ECC71" },
    gui.Box { w = 1, h = 1, color = "#3498DB" },
}

docs.title: gui.AnimatedImage
docs.text:
Shows an image that plays an animation. The texture must contain every frame stacked on top of each other (the first frame at the top), with all frames the same size, like the frames of an animated node texture. So a texture with 3 frames of 16x16 pixels is 16 pixels wide and 48 pixels high. w and h are the size of one displayed frame, and the picture is scaled to that size.

middle_* parameters turn on nine-slice drawing, see Nine-Slice Images. The cuts are measured in pixels of one frame.

The examples use a texture with three frames (red, green, blue), built with texture modifiers ([fill) so no file is needed.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.AnimatedImage {
    w = 2,
    h = 2,

    -- Only useful for styling.
    name = "my_animated_image", -- Optional

    -- Texture that contains all frames, stacked from top to bottom.
    -- This one is 16 pixels wide and 48 high: three frames of 16x16.
    texture_name = "[fill:16x48:white^[fill:12x12:2,2:#E74C3C"
        .. "^[fill:12x12:2,18:#2ECC71^[fill:12x12:2,34:#3498DB",

    -- Number of frames in the texture.
    frame_count = 3,

    -- Milliseconds each frame is shown for. 0 means no animation.
    frame_duration = 500,

    -- Frame to start on, the first frame is 1. Default 1.
    -- This one starts on the green frame.
    frame_start = 2, -- Optional

    -- Nine-slice cuts, in pixels of one frame. Also optional: middle_y,
    -- middle_x2 and middle_y2, see the live example below.
    middle_x = 2, -- Optional
}

docs.title: Live Example
docs.text:
The left one cycles through the frames and the right one is nine-sliced (middle_x = 2). Set frame_duration = 0 to stop on frame_start.

local FRAMES = "[fill:16x48:white^[fill:12x12:2,2:#E74C3C"
    .. "^[fill:12x12:2,18:#2ECC71^[fill:12x12:2,34:#3498DB"

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.HBox {
        gui.AnimatedImage {
            w = 3, h = 3,
            texture_name = FRAMES, frame_count = 3, frame_duration = 500,
        },
        gui.AnimatedImage {
            w = 4, h = 2,
            texture_name = FRAMES, frame_count = 3, frame_duration = 500,
            middle_x = 2,
        },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Background
docs.text:
Draws a picture behind everything else in the form: all backgrounds are drawn before any other element, whatever order they are in. The picture (texture_name) is stretched to w by h. If auto_clip is true, it is cut off at the edge of the form instead and w and h are ignored.

You usually do not need this element, set bgimg on a container or the root element instead (see Padding). Inside a gui.Stack, a gui.ScrollableVBox, or an embedded form, flow draws backgrounds without auto_clip as ordinary images.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The background comes last in the list but is still drawn behind the button.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.Container {
        w = 6, h = 3,
        { type = "button", x = 1.5, y = 1, w = 3, h = 1, label = "In front" },
        {
            type = "background",
            x = 0, y = 0, w = 6, h = 3,
            texture_name = "[fill:16x16:white^[fill:12x12:2,2:#336699",

            -- Cut off at the form edge, ignoring w and h.
            auto_clip = false, -- Optional
        },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Background9
docs.text: Like gui.Background, but the picture is drawn as a nine-slice so that it can be stretched to any size without distorting its corners.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The left background stretches the whole picture, so its border gets thick and blurry. The right one is a gui.Background9, so only the middle stretches.

local FRAME = "[fill:16x16:white^[fill:12x12:2,2:#336699"

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.HBox {
        gui.Container {
            w = 5, h = 3,
            { type = "label", x = 0.5, y = 1.5, label = "Background" },
            { type = "background", x = 0, y = 0, w = 5, h = 3, texture_name = FRAME },
        },
        gui.Container {
            w = 5, h = 3,
            { type = "label", x = 0.5, y = 1.5, label = "Background9" },
            {
                type = "background9",
                x = 0, y = 0, w = 5, h = 3,
                texture_name = FRAME,

                -- Cut 2 pixels from every side. Also optional:
                -- middle_y, middle_x2 and middle_y2.
                middle_x = 2,
            },
        },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Bgcolor
docs.text: Sets the colors behind the form. This does the same thing as the bgcolor, fbgcolor, and bg_fullscreen options of the root element, which are explained in Experimental Features and are easier to use. fullscreen can be false, true, "both", or "neither".

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Pick a color to change the background of the form.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Bgcolor {
            bgcolor = ctx.form.color or "red",

            -- false, true, "both", or "neither".
            fullscreen = false, -- Optional

            -- Color of the area behind the form.
            fbgcolor = "#00000080", -- Optional
        },

        gui.Dropdown {
            name = "color",
            items = { "red", "green", "blue", "purple" },
        },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Box
docs.text:
Draws a solid rectangle of one color. Boxes have no natural size, so give them a w and h.

Unlike everywhere else, a hexadecimal color without an alpha value ("#RGB" or "#RRGGBB") is drawn with an alpha of 8C (140 out of 255, about 55% opaque) here. Add the alpha value ("#FF0000FF") to make it opaque. Color names such as "red" are not affected and are opaque unless you add an alpha value ("red#80"). Flow also draws the bgcolor of gui.HBox, gui.VBox, and other containers with a box, so the same applies to it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The first and last boxes are translucent, the other two are opaque:

gui.HBox {
    -- #RRGGBB gets an alpha of 8C here.
    gui.Box { w = 1, h = 2, color = "#FF0000" },

    -- Add the alpha value to make it opaque.
    gui.Box { w = 1, h = 2, color = "#FF0000FF" },

    -- Color names are opaque unless you add an alpha value.
    gui.Box { w = 1, h = 2, color = "red" },
    gui.Box { w = 1, h = 2, color = "red#80" },
}

docs.title: gui.Button
docs.text:
A clickable button showing label. Your on_event function is called when it is clicked. If you do not set w and h, the button is sized to fit the label (but never smaller than 1.6 by 0.8).

Buttons do not store a value in ctx.form.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Button {
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_button", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ButtonExit
docs.text: A button that closes the form when it is clicked. Your on_event function is still called before the form closes. In all other respects it works like gui.Button.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.ButtonExit {
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_button_exit", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ButtonURL
docs.text: A button that, when clicked, offers the player the choice of opening url in their web browser. url must start with http:// or https://. Your on_event function is also called. In all other respects it works like gui.Button.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.ButtonURL {
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_button_url", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Web address to offer to open.
    url = "https://example.com",
}

docs.title: gui.ButtonUrlExit
docs.text: Like gui.ButtonURL, but the form also closes when the button is clicked. Unlike gui.ButtonURL, it does not get a size from its label, so w and h are required.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.ButtonUrlExit {
    w = 6,
    h = 2,
    name = "my_button_url_exit", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Web address to offer to open.
    url = "https://example.com",
}

docs.title: gui.Checkbox
docs.text:
A tick box with a text label. selected sets whether it starts ticked. If you give it a name, ctx.form[name] is true or false and is updated as soon as the player ticks or unticks it.

Checkboxes are sized automatically and do not accept w or h.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Checkbox {
    name = "my_checkbox", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
    selected = true, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Dropdown
docs.text:
A drop-down list that shows the currently selected item and lets the player pick another one from items (a list of strings). selected_idx is the number of the item that is selected at first (the first item is 1).

ctx.form[name] is the text of the selected item. If index_event = true it is the number of the selected item instead, which is easier to work with when two items have the same text or when the text is translated.

If you do not set w and h, the dropdown is sized to fit its longest item (but never smaller than 2 by 0.8). Item text cannot be coloured.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Dropdown {
    w = 4, -- Optional
    h = 0.8, -- Optional
    name = "my_dropdown", -- Optional

    -- List of choices.
    items = { "Apple", "Banana", "Cherry" },

    -- Number of the item selected at first.
    selected_idx = 2, -- Optional

    -- Store the item number in ctx.form instead of its text.
    index_event = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Field
docs.text:
A single-line text box. label, if set, is shown above the box (flow leaves room for it automatically). default is the text it starts with.

ctx.form[name] is the text in the box. Newlines and other control characters are removed from it, but tabs are kept (a player can only get a newline into a field by pasting). See Security for the exact rules. The text is sent to the server when the player presses a button or Enter. To react to Enter, see Handling Enter Keypresses in Fields.

If you do not set w and h, the field is sized to fit its default text and label (but never smaller than 3 by 0.8).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Field {
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_field", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Text the field starts with.
    default = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Called when the player presses Enter.
    on_key_enter = function(player, ctx) end, -- Optional

    -- Close the form on Enter. Default false.
    close_on_enter = false, -- Optional

    -- Make "Done" on the mobile on-screen keyboard act like Enter.
    enter_after_edit = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.FieldCloseOnEnter
docs.text: Sets whether pressing Enter in the field with this name closes the form. You normally do not need this element, as gui.Field has a close_on_enter parameter (and by default Enter does not close the form).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Type something and press Enter. While the checkbox is ticked, Enter also closes the form.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Field { name = "note", label = "Type something, then press Enter:" },
        gui.FieldCloseOnEnter {
            -- Name of the field.
            name = "note",
            close_on_enter = ctx.form.close or false,
        },
        gui.Checkbox { name = "close", label = "Close the form on Enter" },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.FieldEnterAfterEdit
docs.text: Experimental, and only affects Android. If enter_after_edit is true, pressing "Done" in the text input dialog of the field with this name counts as pressing Enter. You normally do not need this element, as gui.Field has an enter_after_edit parameter.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.VBox {
    gui.Field { name = "msg", label = "Edit me, then press Done" },
    gui.FieldEnterAfterEdit {
        -- Name of the field.
        name = "msg",
        enter_after_edit = true,
    },
}

docs.title: gui.Hypertext
docs.text:
Shows text that can be formatted (bold, colors, different sizes, images, ...) and can contain clickable links. The text is written in a small HTML-like language, which is described in Hypertext Markup. w and h are the size of the area that the text is wrapped to fit in.

If the markup contains <action name=...> links, ctx.form[name] is set to "action:" followed by the action name when the player clicks one. This behaviour is experimental and may change.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Hypertext {
    w = 6,
    h = 2,

    -- Receives the clicked action, see above.
    name = "my_hypertext", -- Optional

    -- Formatted text, see "Hypertext markup".
    text = "<big>Hello</big> <b>bold</b> <i>italic</i> " ..
        "<style color='red'>red</style> world!",
}

docs.title: gui.Image
docs.text: Shows a picture, stretched to fit w by h. If you want to use one small texture for pictures of many sizes, use the middle_* parameters, see Nine-Slice Images.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Image {
    w = 4,
    h = 2,

    -- Texture to draw. This one is a white border around a blue square,
    -- made with texture modifiers so that no file is needed.
    texture_name = "[fill:16x16:white^[fill:12x12:2,2:#336699",

    -- Nine-slice cuts, in pixels of the texture. The border is 2 pixels
    -- wide, so these keep it the same width however big the image is.
    middle_x = 2, -- Optional
    middle_y = 2, -- Optional
    middle_x2 = -2, -- Optional
    middle_y2 = -2, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ImageButton
docs.text:
A button that is drawn as a picture instead of the usual button face. The picture (texture_name) is stretched to w by h, and label is drawn on top of it. It works like gui.Button otherwise.

  • noclip: Allow the button to be drawn outside the form's area.
  • drawborder: Draw the normal button border around the picture.
  • pressed_texture_name: Picture to show while the button is held down.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.ImageButton {
    w = 6,
    h = 2,

    -- Picture to draw as the button. This one is a blue square, made with
    -- a texture modifier so that no file is needed.
    texture_name = "[fill:16x16:#3498DB",
    name = "my_image_button", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
    noclip = false, -- Optional
    drawborder = false, -- Optional

    -- Picture to show while the button is held down (a red square).
    pressed_texture_name = "[fill:16x16:#E74C3C", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ImageButtonExit
docs.text: Like gui.ImageButton, but the form also closes when the button is clicked.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.ImageButtonExit {
    w = 6,
    h = 2,
    texture_name = "[fill:16x16:#3498DB",
    label = "Close", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ItemImage
docs.text: Shows the picture that is used for an item or node in inventories (item_name, such as "unifieddyes:colorium"), stretched to fit w by h.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.ItemImage {
    w = 2,
    h = 2,

    -- Registered item or node name.
    item_name = "unifieddyes:colorium",
}

docs.title: gui.ItemImageButton
docs.text:
A button that shows the inventory picture of an item or node (item_name). By default, the item's description is shown as a tooltip when the player hovers over the button, which you can replace with the tooltip parameter. It works like gui.Button otherwise.

Give every item image button its own unique name, otherwise its tooltip may not work.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.ItemImageButton {
    w = 3,
    h = 2,

    -- Registered item or node name.
    item_name = "unifieddyes:colorium",
    name = "my_item_image_button", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Label
docs.text:
Shows text. Labels do not wrap long lines automatically: use \n to start a new line and do not use labels for long paragraphs. For those, use gui.Hypertext, or a gui.Textarea without a name (which wraps its text and gets a scrollbar if the text is too long).

Labels are sized to fit their text, and flow ignores color escape sequences when it estimates the width. To make the text bigger or smaller, use the font_size style (for example style = {font_size = "*2"}), see Styling.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Label {
    label = "Hello world!",
}

docs.title: gui.List
docs.text:
Shows a grid of inventory slots, with the items of one inventory list in it. This is how you show the player's inventory, a chest, a furnace's input slots, and so on.

  • inventory_location: Which inventory to show. Common values are "current_player" (the inventory of the player who has the form open), "nodemeta:X,Y,Z" (the inventory of the node at that position, for example "nodemeta:10,5,-3"), and "detached:name" (a detached inventory). "player:name" is the inventory of a specific player and is only ever sent to that player.
  • list_name: The name of the list inside that inventory, such as "main" or "craft".
  • w and h: How many slots wide and high to draw (whole numbers).

Slots are filled from left to right, then top to bottom, and the player can move items in and out of them. The list is only shown if the inventory has been sent to the player's client. Only as many slots as the inventory list has are drawn, even if w times h is larger.

Each slot is 1 by 1, with 0.25 between slots, so a list that is 8 slots wide and 4 high is 9.75 by 4.75 big. To change the slot size or spacing, use the size and spacing styles, see Styling.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.List {
    -- Which inventory to show.
    inventory_location = "current_player",

    -- Which list in that inventory to show.
    list_name = "main",
    w = 4,
    h = 2,

    -- Index of the first slot to draw. Unlike most numbers here, this starts
    -- at 0. Default 0.
    starting_item_index = 3, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Listcolors
docs.text:
Sets the colors of inventory slots. It is invisible, takes up no space, and should come before the gui.List elements it is for.

  • slot_bg_normal: Background color of a slot.
  • slot_bg_hover: Background color of a slot while the mouse is over it.
  • slot_border: Color of the border of the slots.
  • tooltip_bgcolor: Default background color of item tooltips.
  • tooltip_fontcolor: Default text color of item tooltips.

Only the first two are required. To use pictures instead of colors for slots, see Unsupported Features.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Pick a theme, then hover over the slots to see both colors.

local themes = {
    Green = { normal = "#2E7D32", hover = "#66BB6A" },
    Blue = { normal = "#1565C0", hover = "#64B5F6" },
    Red = { normal = "#B71C1C", hover = "#EF5350" },
}

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    local theme = themes[ctx.form.theme or "Green"]
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Dropdown { name = "theme", items = { "Green", "Blue", "Red" } },
        gui.Label { label = "Hover over a slot:" },

        -- Color the lists that come after this.
        gui.Listcolors {
            slot_bg_normal = theme.normal,
            slot_bg_hover = theme.hover,
            slot_border = "#FFFFFF", -- Optional
            tooltip_bgcolor = "#000000", -- Optional
            tooltip_fontcolor = "#FFFF00", -- Optional
        },
        gui.List {
            inventory_location = "current_player",
            list_name = "main",
            w = 8, h = 1,
        },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Listring
docs.text:
Sets where items go when the player shift-clicks them. A ring is an ordered list of inventory lists that Luanti keeps for the form, which starts out empty. Every gui.Listring{inventory_location = ..., list_name = ...} adds one list to the end of the ring. When the player shift-clicks an item in a list that is in the ring, the item is sent to the next list in the ring. Lists that are not in the ring keep Luanti's default shift-click behavior.

A list can be added to the ring more than once. Luanti sends an item to the entry after the first entry of its own list, and later entries of the same list are only destinations. In a ring of main, craft, main, output, items from main go to craft, items from craft go to the second main, and items from output wrap around to the first main, so both craft and output send to main.

gui.Listring{} with no parameters adds the last two gui.List elements before it. It is invisible and takes up no space.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Shift-click an item in either list to send it to the other one. Untick the checkbox to remove the ring and go back to Luanti's default.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Checkbox { name = "ring", label = "Link the lists", selected = true },
        gui.List {
            inventory_location = "current_player",
            list_name = "main",
            w = 8, h = 1,
        },
        gui.List {
            inventory_location = "current_player",
            list_name = "craft",
            w = 3, h = 3,
        },

        -- Or name the lists explicitly (both parameters are optional):
        -- gui.Listring { inventory_location = "current_player", list_name = "main" },
        ctx.form.ring ~= false and gui.Listring {} or gui.Nil {},
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Model
docs.text:
Shows a 3D model that the player can turn around with their mouse.

  • mesh: File name of the model, from the models folder of any loaded mod.
  • textures: The textures for the model, one for each of the model's materials in order.
  • rotation_x and rotation_y: How far the model is turned at first, in degrees.
  • continuous: Keep the model rotating by itself.
  • mouse_control: Whether the player can rotate the model with their mouse. Defaults to true.
  • frame_loop_begin and frame_loop_end: The range of animation frames to play. Defaults to all frames.
  • animation_speed: Frames per second to play the animation at. Defaults to 0 (no animation).

name is optional and only useful for styling.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Model {
    w = 5,
    h = 5,
    padding = 0.5,

    -- Only useful for styling.
    name = "my_model", -- Optional

    -- Model file name.
    mesh = "voxelmodel.obj",

    -- One texture for each material of the model. This one is a blue
    -- square, made with a texture modifier so that no file is needed.
    textures = { "[fill:16x16:#3498DB^[fill:8x8,0,4:#888888" },

    -- Starting rotation in degrees. This tilts the model so that you can
    -- see it is 3D.
    rotation_x = -20, -- Optional

    -- Starting rotation in degrees.
    rotation_y = 30, -- Optional

    -- Keep rotating by itself. Default false.
    continuous = true, -- Optional

    -- Let the player rotate the model. Default true.
    mouse_control = true, -- Optional

    -- First animation frame to play.
    frame_loop_begin = 5, -- Optional

    -- Last animation frame to play.
    frame_loop_end = 6, -- Optional

    -- Frames per second. Default 0.
    animation_speed = 7, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Pwdfield
docs.text: A single-line text box for passwords: what the player types is hidden. It works like gui.Field, apart from not having a default. ctx.form[name] is the text that was typed. on_key_enter is supported, see Handling Enter Keypresses in Fields.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Pwdfield {
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_pwdfield", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Called when the player presses Enter.
    on_key_enter = function(player, ctx) end, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ScrollContainer
docs.text:
An area of a fixed size that clips the elements inside it and moves them when a scrollbar is moved. You usually want gui.ScrollableVBox instead, which does all of this for you. The elements inside are positioned by hand with x and y, like in gui.Container.

  • w and h: The size of the visible area.
  • scrollbar_name: The name of the gui.Scrollbar that controls the area. You need to add that scrollbar yourself.
  • orientation: "vertical" (the default) or "horizontal".
  • scroll_factor: How far the contents move for each step of the scrollbar's value. Default 0.1. It cannot be negative.

Flow cannot work out the scrollbar range here, so set it with gui.ScrollbarOptions before the scrollbar (whole numbers):

  • max = (content_height - h) / scroll_factor
  • thumbsize = max * h / content_height

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.HBox {
    gui.ScrollContainer {
        w = 4, h = 3,
        scrollbar_name = "my_scrollbar",
        orientation = "vertical",
        { type = "label", x = 0, y = 0.5, label = "Top" },
        { type = "label", x = 0, y = 7.5, label = "Bottom" },
    },

    -- Contents are 8 high with 3 visible: max = 5 / 0.1 = 50 and
    -- thumbsize = 50 * 3 / 8 = 18.75, rounded to 19.
    gui.ScrollbarOptions { opts = { max = "50", thumbsize = "19" } },
    gui.Scrollbar {
        w = 0.5, h = 3,
        orientation = "vertical",
        name = "my_scrollbar",
    },
}

docs.title: gui.Scrollbar
docs.text: A slider that the player can drag. ctx.form[name] is its position, a whole number from min to max (by default 0 to 1000, change them with gui.ScrollbarOptions before the scrollbar). value is the position it starts at, and orientation is "vertical" or "horizontal". Use it with a gui.ScrollContainer, or by itself as a slider.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Scrollbar {
    w = 0.6,
    h = 4,

    -- "vertical" or "horizontal".
    orientation = "vertical",
    name = "my_scrollbar", -- Optional

    -- Starting position, from 0 to 1000 by default.
    value = 300, -- Optional
}

Do not use the scrollbar_bg, slider, arrow_up, and arrow_down texture parameters: Luanti has no such parameters, and on Luanti 5.8 and newer a scrollbar that sets any of them is not shown at all. See Scrollbar Textures Do Not Work.

docs.title: gui.ScrollbarOptions
docs.text:
Sets the options of the gui.Scrollbar elements that come after it. It is invisible and takes up no space. opts is a table with any of these options, all values are strings that contain whole numbers (except arrows):

  • min: The smallest value (default 0).
  • max: The largest value (default 1000). If it is the same as min, the scrollbar is disabled.
  • smallstep: How much the value changes when an arrow is clicked or the mouse wheel is scrolled (default 10). A negative number resets it to 10.
  • largestep: How much the value changes for Page Up and Page Down (default 100). A negative number resets it to 100.
  • thumbsize: The size of the thumb (the part that is dragged), counted in values out of the range of the scrollbar. For a scrollbar from 1 to 100, a thumbsize of 10 makes the thumb a tenth of the scrollbar long. If it is zero or less, it is reset to 1.
  • arrows: "show" or "hide" the arrow buttons. "default" hides them if the scrollbar gets too small, and shows them otherwise.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Drag the scrollbar or click the arrows. The value is limited to 0-100 and changes in steps of 5.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Label { label = "Volume: " .. (ctx.form.volume or 0) },

        -- Set the range and steps of the scrollbar below. Also accepts
        -- thumbsize, see the list above.
        gui.ScrollbarOptions {
            opts = {
                min = "0", max = "100",
                smallstep = "5", largestep = "20",
                arrows = ctx.form.arrows and "show" or "hide",
            },
        },
        gui.Scrollbar {
            name = "volume",
            orientation = "horizontal",
            w = 6, h = 0.6,
        },

        gui.Checkbox { name = "arrows", label = "Show arrow buttons" },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.SetFocus
docs.text:
Gives keyboard focus to the element with this name. Put it before that element. Normally the focus is not changed when the form is shown again (for example by form:update()), so that the focus the player chose is kept. Set force to true to move the focus every time.

Checkboxes, buttons (of all kinds), tables, text lists, dropdowns, fields, password fields, text areas, and scrollbars can be focused.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Pick a field in the dropdown and the keyboard focus jumps to it.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        -- Focus the picked field. With force = false (the default),
        -- the focus only moves when the form is first shown.
        gui.SetFocus { name = ctx.form.target or "first", force = true },

        gui.Dropdown { name = "target", items = { "first", "second", "third" } },
        gui.Field { name = "first", label = "First field" },
        gui.Field { name = "second", label = "Second field" },
        gui.Field { name = "third", label = "Third field" },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Style
docs.text: Sets style properties of elements by their name. See Styling. It is invisible and takes up no space.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Pick a color to tint the button named "fancy". The other button is not affected.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Dropdown { name = "color", items = { "red", "green", "blue" } },

        -- Style only the element named "fancy".
        gui.Style {
            selectors = { "fancy" },
            props = { bgcolor = ctx.form.color or "red", textcolor = "yellow" },
        },
        gui.Button { name = "fancy", label = "Styled button" },
        gui.Button { name = "plain", label = "Plain button" },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.StyleType
docs.text: Sets style properties of every element of a type. See Styling. It is invisible and takes up no space.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Pick a text color. Every button after the style changes, but the label does not.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Dropdown { name = "color", items = { "yellow", "orange", "cyan" } },

        -- Color the text of every button that comes after this.
        gui.StyleType {
            selectors = { "button" },
            props = { textcolor = ctx.form.color or "yellow" },
        },
        gui.Button { label = "Button A" },
        gui.Button { label = "Button B" },
        gui.Label { label = "I am a label, so I am not affected." },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Tabheader
docs.text:
A row of tabs. captions is the text of each tab, ctx.form[name] is the number of the selected tab (the first tab is 1), and current_tab is the tab that is selected at first. Showing the right contents for the selected tab is up to you, usually by reading ctx.form[name] in your build function.

Give it both a w and an h: flow cannot work out how much space it needs. If transparent is true the tabs are semi-transparent, and draw_border draws a thin line along the bottom of the tabs.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Tabheader {
    w = 6,
    h = 0.8,
    name = "my_tabheader", -- Optional

    -- Text of each tab.
    captions = { "General", "Video", "Audio" },

    -- Tab selected at first, the first is 1.
    current_tab = 2, -- Optional

    -- Draw semi-transparent. Default false.
    transparent = false, -- Optional

    -- Draw a line along the tabs. Default false.
    draw_border = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Table
docs.text:
A table with rows and columns that scrolls if it has too many rows. The player can select one row, and ctx.form[name] is the number of the selected row (the first row is 1). selected_idx is the row that is selected at first.

cells is one flat list with the text of every cell, going left to right along each row and then down to the next row. The number of columns comes from gui.TableColumns (the default is one text column). Put gui.TableColumns and gui.TableOptions before the table, as they only affect the table that comes after them. They do not take up any space.

Tables have no natural size, so you must give them a w and h.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Table {
    w = 4,
    h = 2,
    name = "my_table", -- Optional

    -- Text of every cell, row by row. There is one column by default, so
    -- this is four rows.
    cells = { "Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave" },

    -- Row selected at first, the first row is 1.
    selected_idx = 3, -- Optional
}

docs.title: Example With Columns and Options
docs.text:
gui.VBox {
    gui.TableColumns {
        tablecolumns = {
            { type = "text", opts = { width = "8" } },
            { type = "text", opts = { align = "right" } },
        },
    },
    gui.TableOptions {
        opts = { highlight = "#335577" },
    },
    gui.Table {
        w = 10, h = 4,
        name = "scores",
        cells = {
            "Alice", "10",
            "Bob", "7",
        },
    },
}

docs.title: gui.TableColumns
docs.text:
Sets the columns of the gui.Table that follows it. tablecolumns is a list with one {type = ..., opts = {...}} entry for each column, from left to right. type is one of:

  • "text": Show the cell contents as text.
  • "image": The cell contents are a number that picks an image, which you set with the options ["0"] = "texture.png", ["1"] = "other.png", and so on (the numbers do not have to be consecutive). Empty cells and cells that are not numbers use image 0. Images are scaled down to fit the height of the row if necessary.
  • "color": The cell contents are a color that is used for the text of the next column(s). Use the span option to set how many columns it affects (default: all remaining columns).
  • "indent": The cell contents are a number that sets how far the next column is indented.
  • "tree": Like "indent", but the player can open and close the indented rows, like in a file browser.

opts is a table of options, all values are strings. width and padding are measured in "em" units (relative to the font size), unlike most other sizes in flow, which are in slot units:

  • align: For text and image columns, where the content goes in the cell: "left" (default), "center", "right", or "inline".
  • width: For text and image columns, the minimum width, in "em" units (relative to the font size, default 0). For indent and tree columns, how far each level is indented (default 1.5).
  • padding: Space to the left of the column, in "em" units (default 0.5, or 0 for indent columns).
  • tooltip: Text to show when hovering over the column.
  • span: For color columns, how many of the following columns the color affects (default: all remaining columns).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
See also Example With Indent and Tree Columns. Pick an alignment for the last column and select a row. The middle column colors the text of the last one.

local names = { "Alice", "Bob", "Carol" }

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Dropdown { name = "align", items = { "left", "center", "right", "inline" } },

        -- Set the columns of the table below.
        gui.TableColumns {
            tablecolumns = {
                { type = "text", opts = { width = "8" } },
                { type = "color", opts = {} },
                { type = "text", opts = { align = ctx.form.align or "left" } },
            },
        },
        gui.Table {
            w = 6, h = 3,
            name = "scores",
            cells = {
                "Alice", "#66FF66", "10",
                "Bob", "#FFFF66", "7",
                "Carol", "#FF6666", "3",
            },
        },

        gui.Label { label = "Selected: " .. names[ctx.form.scores or 1] },
    }
end)

docs.title: Example With Indent and Tree Columns
docs.text:
An "indent" or "tree" column takes one cell in every row, like any other column, but the cell is not shown. It holds the level of the row: "0" for the leftmost level, "1" for the next one, and so on (a negative number counts as 0). The column after it is moved to the right by the level times the width option of the indent or tree column, so put the text you want to show in that next column.

gui.VBox {
    gui.TableColumns {
        tablecolumns = {
            -- The level of each row. It is not shown.
            { type = "tree", opts = {} },
            -- The text of each row.
            { type = "text", opts = { width = "8" } },
        },
    },
    gui.TableOptions {
        -- Open the rows of level 0 at first.
        opts = { opendepth = "1" },
    },
    gui.Table {
        w = 5, h = 3,
        name = "files",
        cells = {
            "0", "Fruit",
            "1", "Apple",
            "1", "Banana",
            "0", "Vegetables",
            "1", "Carrot",
        },
    },
}

Each row is its level, then its text. Apple and Banana are one level deeper than Fruit, so they are indented and belong to it.

With "tree", a parent row shows a - (open) or + (closed) that the player clicks, or they double-click the row, to open or close the rows below it. opendepth = "1" in gui.TableOptions opens level 0 at first, otherwise only Fruit and Vegetables are visible. The selected row in ctx.form.files is the position in cells, so Carrot is 5 even when the rows above it are closed.

With "indent", rows are indented the same way, but there is no sign and every row is always visible.

docs.title: gui.TableOptions
docs.text:
Sets the appearance of the gui.Table that follows it. opts is a table with any of these options, all values are strings:

  • color: Default text color (default "#FFFFFF").
  • background: Background color of the table (default "#000000").
  • border: "true" or "false", whether to draw a border (default "true").
  • highlight: Background color of the selected row (default "#466432").
  • highlight_text: Text color of the selected row (default "#FFFFFF").
  • opendepth: How many levels of "tree" column rows are open at first. Rows deeper than this are collapsed (default "0"). See Example With Indent and Tree Columns.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Pick a highlight color, select a row, and tick or untick the border.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Dropdown { name = "highlight", items = { "#335577", "#775533", "#337755" } },
        gui.Checkbox { name = "border", label = "Draw a border", selected = true },

        -- Style the table below.
        gui.TableOptions {
            opts = {
                background = "#222222",
                highlight = ctx.form.highlight or "#335577",
                border = tostring(ctx.form.border ~= false),
            },
        },
        gui.Table {
            w = 4, h = 3,
            name = "names",
            cells = { "Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave" },
        },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Textarea
docs.text:
A multi-line text box. Long lines are wrapped to fit the width, and a scrollbar is added if the text is too tall. label, if set, is shown above the box and default is the text it starts with. ctx.form[name] is the text in the box, including its newlines.

Without a name, a textarea is not editable

If you leave out name, the text cannot be edited and no box is drawn, which makes the textarea a label that wraps text and scrolls. This is easy to do by accident when you copy an example. It is also the way to show long text that wraps, because gui.Label does not wrap, see Unsupported Features. Because it wraps, you should set a w and h for this.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Textarea {
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_textarea", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Text the box starts with.
    default = "Hello world!", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Textlist
docs.text:
A list of text rows that scrolls if there are too many to fit. The player can select a row, and ctx.form[name] is the number of the selected row (the first row is 1). selected_idx is the row that is selected at first.

listelems is the text of each row. To color a row, start it with #RRGGBB (six hexadecimal digits). To start a row with a literal #, write ##. If transparent is true, no background is drawn behind the list.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Textlist {
    w = 4, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_textlist", -- Optional

    -- Text of each row. The second row is orange because it starts with a
    -- color, and the third starts with a literal #.
    listelems = { "Plain row", "#FF8800Orange row", "##Hash row", "Last row" },

    -- Row selected at first, the first row is 1.
    selected_idx = 3, -- Optional

    -- Do not draw a background. Default false.
    transparent = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Tooltip
docs.text:
Sets the text that is shown when the player hovers over another element, and optionally the colors of that tooltip. gui_element_name is the name of that element. Put the tooltip after the element it belongs to. It is invisible and does not take up any space.

If you only need to add some text, use the tooltip parameter on the element itself, see Tooltips.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Hover over the button to see the tooltip. Click it and hover again: the text has changed.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Button {
            name = "my_button",
            label = "Click me, then hover",
            on_event = function(player, ctx)
                ctx.clicks = (ctx.clicks or 0) + 1
                return true -- redraw
            end,
        },
        gui.Tooltip {
            -- Name of the element to attach to.
            gui_element_name = "my_button",
            tooltip_text = ("Clicked %d times"):format(ctx.clicks or 0),
            bgcolor = "#000000", -- Optional
            fontcolor = "#FFFF00", -- Optional
        },
    }
end)

docs.title: gui.Vertlabel
docs.text: Shows text vertically, with one letter below the other, from top to bottom.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Vertlabel {
    label = "Hello world!",
}

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: A form is a menu that is shown to a player. It is made of elements (also called widgets), such as labels, buttons, text fields, and inventory slots, which are arranged by layout elements like gui.VBox. You describe a form with a build function, which is the function you pass to flow.make_gui(). It returns the elements, and flow works out the positions and sizes and shows the form for you. This documentation always calls it the build function. See Functional Elements for what each element does.

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
See example.lua in the flow repository for a more comprehensive example which demonstrates how layouting and alignment works. In singleplayer, a player with the server privilege can also run /flow-example to open it in the game.

The build function is called with the player and a context table (ctx) every time the form is drawn. ctx belongs to one player's copy of the form: flow keeps the same table for as long as the form is open, passes it to the build function and to every on_event function, and you can store anything in it. Flow adds a ctx.form table to it, which holds the current values of the form's named inputs (see Names and Values).

Three things in the example below look alike but differ:

Name in the example What it is Who writes it ctx.value The starting ctx: whatever you passed to form:show. You, before the form is shown. ctx.form.cool_dropdown The live value of the input named cool_dropdown. Flow: it sets the initial value on the first draw and updates it when the player changes the input. ctx.picked Your own state. Your on_event function, when the player presses the button.

All three are in the same table. Do not use form as a key of your own or replace ctx.form: flow raises an error if you do that in the build function.

form:show(player, ctx) shows the form to a player. Flow uses the ctx table you pass as is (not a copy), or a new empty one if you leave it out. In a mod, get the player object from a chat command or core.register_on_joinplayer.

local gui = flow.widgets -- local recommended for direct referencing
local STARTING_SELECTION = 3 -- change and rerun to see the difference

local function build_vbox(player_obj, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Label { label = "Here is a dropdown:" },
        gui.Dropdown {
            name = "cool_dropdown",
            items = { 'First item', 'Second item', 'Third item' },
            index_event = true,
            selected_idx = ctx.value or 1
        },
        gui.Button {
            label = "Get dropdown index",
            on_event = function(player, ctx)
                local idx = ctx.form.cool_dropdown or ctx.value or 1
                core.chat_send_player(player:get_player_name(),
                    ("You have selected item #%d!"):format(idx))

                -- Remember the index and redraw so the label below shows it.
                ctx.picked = idx
                return true
            end,
        },
        gui.Label {
            label = ctx.picked
                and ("You have selected item #%d!"):format(ctx.picked)
                or "Pick an item, then press the button.",
        },
    }
end

local form = flow.make_gui(build_vbox)
-- "singleplayer" is the default player name for single-player games
local player_obj = core.get_player_by_name("singleplayer")

form:show(player_obj, { value = STARTING_SELECTION }) -- Starting ctx, optional

Pick an item and press the button: the button's on_event function stores the index in ctx.picked and returns true, which redraws the form so that the label under the button changes. The same message is also sent to the chat.

docs.title: Updating Forms
docs.text:
If some data displayed inside a form changes (for example a timer or progress indicator), you can use my_gui:update(player) or my_gui:update_where(func) (see below) to update the form without resetting ctx or showing the form again if the player has closed it.

Luanti has no way to change a form that is already open, so flow has to show the whole form again. Because of this, players may lose text typed into fields that hasn't been sent to the server (which happens when they press a button or Enter) when the form is updated.

Here is a form with one button for each way to update it. The counter is a plain variable, not something stored in ctx, so flow cannot notice when it changes. Each button adds 1 to it and then redraws the forms that should show the new number.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
local gui = flow.widgets
local counter = 0 -- External state; flow cannot track its changes.
local my_gui

local function add_button(label, update)
    return gui.Button {
        label = label,
        on_event = function(player, ctx)
            counter = counter + 1
            update(player, ctx)
        end,
    }
end

my_gui = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    ctx.test = 123 -- Used by update_where() below.
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Label { label = "Counter: " .. counter },
        add_button("Add 1 and update my form", function(p)
            my_gui:update(p)
        end),
