        add_button("Add 1 and update forms with ctx.test == 123", function()
            my_gui:update_where(function(_, c) return c.test == 123 end)
        end),
        add_button("Add 1 and update forms of admins", function()
            my_gui:update_where(function(p)
                return core.check_player_privs(p:get_player_name(), "server")
            end)
        end),
        add_button("Add 1 and update everyone's form", function()
            my_gui:update_where(function() return true end)
        end),
    }
end)

Inside an on_event handler, you can return true instead of calling my_gui:update(player), as the click counter example below does.

If you're using a form as a HUD, you must call my_gui:show_hud(player) to update it. See HUDs for how to show and close one.

Updating a form does not reset ctx. In this example a timer redraws every open copy of the form each second, while the click counter stored in ctx survives every redraw:

local gui = flow.widgets
local seconds = 0 -- Shared by every open copy of the form.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Label { label = ("Form drawn after %d seconds"):format(seconds) },
        gui.Label { label = ("Clicks (kept in ctx): %d"):format(ctx.clicks or 0) },
        gui.Button {
            label = "Click me",
            on_event = function(player, ctx)
                ctx.clicks = (ctx.clicks or 0) + 1
                return true -- redraw this form
            end,
        },
    }
end)

local function tick()
    seconds = seconds + 1
    form:update_where(function() return true end)
    core.after(1, tick)
end
core.after(1, tick)

form:show(core.get_player_by_name("current_player"))

docs.title: Redrawing When a Value Changes
docs.text:
You often do not need return true. If your build function reads the value of a named input from ctx.form, flow notices and redraws the form by itself whenever the player changes that value.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Checkbox { name = "advanced", label = "Show advanced options", selected = true },

        -- Reading ctx.form.advanced here makes flow redraw the form
        -- whenever the checkbox changes.
        ctx.form.advanced and gui.Label { label = "Advanced options" }
            or gui.Nil {},
    }
end)

The rules are:

  • Only reads while the build function runs count, including reads in helper functions that it calls. Reading ctx.form inside an on_event function does not.
  • The form is only redrawn if the value is different from the stored one.
  • If the element has its own on_event function, there is no automatic redraw. That function has to return true instead.
  • Text fields only send their text when the player presses a button or Enter (see Names and Values), so the redraw happens then, and only if the text is different from the stored one. Pressing a button with the text unchanged does not redraw because of the field.

Here are the two cases that surprise people. Only Show details redraws the form when ticked:

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        -- No on_event, and the build function reads it below: ticking
        -- this redraws the form.
        gui.Checkbox { name = "details", label = "Show details" },

        -- Has its own on_event: ticking this does NOT redraw the form
        -- unless the function returns true.
        gui.Checkbox {
            name = "loud", label = "Loud",
            on_event = function(player, ctx) end,
        },

        gui.Label {
            label = ("details = %s, loud = %s"):format(
                tostring(ctx.form.details), tostring(ctx.form.loud)),
        },
    }
end)

docs.title: Context and Redraws at a Glance
Context Lifetime by Mode
docs.text:
How long ctx lives depends on how the form is shown:

How the form is shown Where ctx comes from How long it is kept my_gui:show(player, ctx) The table you pass, or a new empty one. Until the form is closed. update, update_where and return true keep it. Calling show again starts with a new one. my_gui:set_as_inventory_for(player, ctx), see Inventory The table you pass. If you pass none and this form is already the player's inventory, the existing ctx is reused, otherwise a new empty one. Until the form is unset or the player leaves. Passing a new ctx replaces the old one. my_gui:show_hud(player, ctx), see HUDs The table you pass, or a new empty one every time. Not kept: flow remembers nothing between calls, so pass your own table each time. my_gui:render_to_formspec_string(player, ctx), see Rendering to a Formspec The table you pass, or a new empty one. Flow keeps nothing: pass the same ctx each time you redraw.

docs.title: Ways to Redraw a Form
docs.text: Way Redraws Keeps ctx Works for return true from on_event or on_key_enter The form of the player who used it Yes Forms shown with show and inventory forms Reading ctx.form.name in the build function (see Redrawing When a Value Changes) The form of the player who changed the value Yes Forms shown with show and inventory forms my_gui:update(player) One player, if they have the form open Yes Forms shown with show only my_gui:update_where(func) Every player with the form open for whom func(player, ctx) returns true Yes Forms shown with show only my_gui:set_as_inventory_for(player, ctx) One player Reused if you pass none Inventory forms only my_gui:show_hud(player, ctx) One player No HUDs only my_gui:show(player, ctx) One player (and the old form is replaced) No, starts from the ctx you pass Forms shown with show

docs.title: Hiding Elements
docs.text: Elements inside boxes can have visible = false set to hide them from the player. Elements hidden this way will still take up space like with visibility: hidden; in CSS.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Untick the checkbox to hide the middle button: it disappears, but the gap it leaves stays.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Checkbox { name = "show", label = "Show the middle button", selected = true },
        gui.Button { label = "First button" },
        gui.Button { label = "Middle button", visible = ctx.form.show ~= false },
        gui.Button { label = "Last button" },
    }
end)

docs.title: Where It Works
docs.text:
• visible = false works on elements inside gui.HBox, gui.VBox, gui.Stack, gui.ScrollableVBox, and gui.PaginatedVBox. In a gui.Stack, the hidden element still counts towards the size of the stack.
  • It does nothing on elements placed directly inside a gui.Container or gui.ScrollContainer (the ones you position yourself with x and y): they are still drawn. See Manual Positioning.
  • It does nothing on the root element of the form, which is always shown.

docs.title: What Happens to Hidden Elements
docs.text:
Flow takes a hidden element out of the form after it has worked out the layout, and before it handles anything else. The player's client never receives it, so:

  • A hidden button cannot be clicked or focused, and its on_event function is never called. The same goes for every other hidden element.
  • Its style and tooltip are not sent either.
  • A hidden input with a name is not registered, so flow does not set or update ctx.form[name] while it is hidden. A value that is already in ctx.form is kept and is applied again when the element is shown.

Type something in the field of this example, then untick the checkbox. The field disappears, but the label still shows what you typed, and the text is back in the field when you tick the checkbox again:

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Checkbox { name = "show_note", label = "Show the note field", selected = true },
        gui.Field { name = "note", label = "Note", visible = ctx.form.show_note ~= false },
        gui.Label { label = "Stored note: " .. (ctx.form.note or "") },
    }
end)

While the field is hidden, flow ignores a note value sent by the client, because the field is not registered.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: If you don't want hidden elements to take up any space, see the documentation for gui.Nil. gui.Nil is an invisible element (a tooltip) that is hidden with visible = false, so it is skipped when the layout is worked out. See Invisible Elements for the others. An invisible element that is itself given visible = false is removed from the form in the same way, it just never had a size.

docs.title: Using a Form as a HUD
docs.text:
A form can be shown as a HUD (text and pictures drawn over the game screen) instead of a menu. A HUD cannot be clicked or typed into, so it is only useful for showing information such as a score, a timer, or a status display.

Flow uses the hud_fs mod to do this. It is an optional dependency, so it must be installed separately. hud_fs only draws some of the formspec elements, and ignores the others, see its page for the list.

docs.title: Showing and Closing a HUD
docs.text:
local gui = flow.widgets
local player = core.get_player_by_name("current_player")

local my_gui = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        -- Put the HUD in the top-right corner.
        window_position = { x = 1, y = 0 },
        window_anchor = { x = 1, y = 0 },

        gui.Label { label = ctx.text },
    }
end)

-- Draw the form as a HUD, or redraw it if it is already shown.
my_gui:show_hud(player, { text = "I am a HUD!" })

-- Remove the HUD again after 5 seconds.
core.after(5, function()
    my_gui:close_hud(player)
end)
  • show_hud(player, ctx) draws the form as a HUD, or redraws it if it is already shown. Without hud_fs it stops with an error. ctx is optional.
  • close_hud(player) removes the HUD.

Flow does not keep a context for HUDs. If you leave out ctx, show_hud uses a new empty table every time it is called, so keep your own table and pass it each time if the form needs to remember anything. This is different from inventory forms, which reuse their context. The table in Context Lifetime by Mode compares all the ways of showing a form.

docs.title: Updating a HUD
docs.text: my_gui:update(player) and my_gui:update_where(func) only affect forms shown with my_gui:show(player), so they do nothing to a HUD. Call show_hud again to update it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
local gui = flow.widgets

local hud = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        -- Put the HUD in the top-right corner.
        window_position = { x = 1, y = 0 },
        window_anchor = { x = 1, y = 0 },

        gui.Label { label = "Score: " .. ctx.score },
    }
end)

local contexts = {}

local function set_score(player, score)
    local name = player:get_player_name()
    contexts[name] = contexts[name] or {}
    local ctx = contexts[name]
    ctx.score = score

    if not ctx.hidden then
        -- Pass the same context every time.
        hud:show_hud(player, ctx)
    end
end

core.register_on_joinplayer(function(player)
    set_score(player, 0)
end)

core.register_on_leaveplayer(function(player)
    contexts[player:get_player_name()] = nil
end)

-- Add a point every second so the HUD visibly changes.
local timer = 0
core.register_globalstep(function(dtime)
    timer = timer + dtime
    if timer < 1 then return end
    timer = 0

    for _, player in ipairs(core.get_connected_players()) do
        local ctx = contexts[player:get_player_name()]
        if ctx then
            set_score(player, ctx.score + 1)
        end
    end
end)

-- /hud off removes the HUD, /hud on brings it back.
core.register_chatcommand("hud", {
    params = "<on|off>",
    description = "Show or hide the score HUD",
    func = function(name, param)
        local player = core.get_player_by_name(name)
        local ctx = contexts[name]
        if not player or not ctx then return end

        if param == "off" then
            ctx.hidden = true
            hud:close_hud(player)
        else
            ctx.hidden = nil
            hud:show_hud(player, ctx)
        end
    end,
})

The score in the top-right corner goes up by one every second. Run /hud off to remove it with close_hud and /hud on to show it again with show_hud.

docs.title: Things to Know
docs.text:
• No input. on_event and on_key_enter functions are never called, as the player cannot use a HUD.
  • Position and size. Use window_position, window_anchor, and window_padding on the root element to place the HUD, see Experimental Features.
  • Scrolling. Flow does not know the player's formspec version when it draws a HUD, so it treats the player as an old client. gui.ScrollableVBox becomes a gui.PaginatedVBox, whose page buttons do nothing in a HUD. Avoid both of them.

docs.title: Hypertext Markup
docs.text:
gui.Hypertext shows text that is written in a small markup language with tags that look like HTML tags. It can be used to make text bold, coloured, bigger, or centred, to add pictures, and to add clickable links.

The markup language is defined by Luanti, see Markup Language in the Luanti API documentation.

Warning: The markup language is currently unstable and may change. Use it with caution. Flow passes the text to Luanti without looking at it, so everything on this page is handled by the player's Luanti client, not by flow.

gui.Hypertext {
    w = 8, h = 3,
    text = "<center><big>Welcome!</big></center>" ..
        "This is <b>bold</b>, <i>italic</i>, and " ..
        "<style color='red'>red</style> text.",
}

What flow does not have: the markup can only be used in gui.Hypertext. Luanti can also show it in a tooltip (hypertip[]), but flow has no element for that, see Unsupported Features. Colors in the markup are written like colors everywhere else, see Colors: the client reads them with the same code, so #RGB, #RRGGBB, #RGBA, #RRGGBBAA, color names, and a name with an alpha value (red#80) all work. A color without an alpha value is fully opaque, and a color the client cannot read is ignored.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Some tags enclose text: they open with <tagname> and close with </tagname>. Tags can have attributes, which are written in the opening tag as key=value. Attribute values should be quoted with either " or '. Inside a Lua string that is already in double quotes, use single quotes, as in <style color='red'>.

To write a literal <, >, or \ in the text, put a backslash before it. In a quoted attribute value, put a backslash before a literal quote mark. In Lua code, each backslash has to be written twice ("\\<"), or you can use a long string ([[\<]]).

docs.title: <style color=... font=... size=...>...</style>
docs.text:
Changes the style of the text inside it.

  • color: Text color.
  • size: Text size, a whole number where 16 is the normal size (the size the player chose in their settings), so 32 is twice as big and 8 is half as big. <big> is 24 and <bigger> is 36. The relative values from Styling are not supported: *1.5 is ignored and +2 is read as plain 2.
  • font: Text font, mono or normal.

docs.title: <global ...>
docs.text:
Sets the style of the whole text. You only need to use it once. If you put several in the text, their changes are made in the order the tags appear.

Attributes that only apply to the whole text:

  • background: Background of the text, a color or none.
  • margin: Space around the edge of the text, in pixels.
  • valign: Vertical alignment of the text: top, middle, or bottom.

Attributes that are inherited by everything inside the text:

  • color: Default text color.
  • hovercolor: Color of <action> links while the mouse is over them.
  • size: Default text size, written like size in <style>.
  • font: Default font, mono or normal.
  • halign: Default horizontal alignment: left, right, center, or justify.

docs.title: <tag name=... color=... hovercolor=... font=... size=...>
docs.text:
Defines a new tag, or changes the style of an existing one.

  • name: The name of the tag to define or change.
  • color: Text color.
  • hovercolor: Text color while the mouse is over it (only for action tags).
  • size: Text size, written like size in <style>.
  • font: Text font, mono or normal.

docs.title: Layout Tags
docs.text:
These tags are always available. You can add more with <tag ...>.

Tag Effect <normal>...</normal> Normal size text <big>...</big> Big text <bigger>...</bigger> Bigger text <center>...</center> Centred text <left>...</left> Left-aligned text <right>...</right> Right-aligned text <justify>...</justify> Justified text <mono>...</mono> Monospaced font <b>...</b>, <i>...</i>, <u>...</u> Bold, italic, and underlined text

docs.title: <action name=...>...</action>
docs.text:
Makes the text inside it clickable. name is required. An optional url attribute is a web address to open when the text is clicked.

When the player clicks it, the form is sent to the server and the value of the gui.Hypertext element is "action:" followed by the action name. In flow, give the element a name and an on_event function, and read the value from ctx.form. This is experimental and may change.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Hypertext {
            w = 6, h = 1,
            name = "help",
            text = "Read the <action name='rules'>rules</action> or the " ..
                "<action name='faq'>FAQ</action>.",
            on_event = function(player, ctx)
                if ctx.form.help == "action:rules" then
                    ctx.reply = "No rules!"
                elseif ctx.form.help == "action:faq" then
                    ctx.reply = "Nobody has asked yet."
                end
                return true -- redraw to show the reply
            end,
        },
        gui.Label { label = ctx.reply or "Click a link." },
    }
end)

docs.title: <img name=... float=... width=... height=...>
docs.text:
Draws a texture that is in the client's media cache.

  • name: The name of the texture (required).
  • float: If present, the picture floats to the left or right and the text flows around it.
  • width, height: Force a size instead of using the size of the texture. If you only give one of them, the shape of the texture is kept.

docs.title: <item name=... float=... width=... height=... rotate=... angle=...>
docs.text:
Draws the inventory picture of an item.

  • name: The item name (required), such as unifieddyes:colorium.
  • float, width, height: Like for <img>.
  • rotate: Make the item turn. Either yes or X,Y,Z, the rotation speeds around each axis as percentages of the standard speed (-1000 to 1000).
  • angle: The angle the item is shown at, as X,Y,Z, the angles around each of the three axes.

rotate and angle only work if the player has the inventory_items_animations setting turned on.

docs.title: Using a Form as an Inventory
docs.text:
A form can be set as the player inventory, which is the screen the player sees when they open their inventory. Flow internally generates the formspec (the text Luanti uses to describe a menu) and passes it to player:set_inventory_formspec(). This will completely replace your inventory and isn't compatible with inventory mods like sfinv (the inventory in Minetest Game, which lets mods add tabs). To put a flow form inside an sfinv-style inventory instead, see Rendering to a Formspec.

Consider using Sway instead if you want to use flow as an inventory replacement while still having some way for other mods to extend the inventory.

local gui = flow.widgets

local example_inventory = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Label { label = ctx.title or "Inventory goes here!" },
        gui.Label { label = "Button clicks: " .. (ctx.clicks or 0) },
        gui.Button {
            label = "Click me",
            on_event = function(player, ctx)
                ctx.clicks = (ctx.clicks or 0) + 1
                return true -- redraw
            end,
        },
    }
end)
core.register_on_joinplayer(function(player)
    example_inventory:set_as_inventory_for(player)
end)

-- /inv_title <text> changes the title, see below.
core.register_chatcommand("inv_title", {
    params = "<text>",
    description = "Change the title of your inventory form",
    func = function(name, param)
        local player = core.get_player_by_name(name)
        if player then
            example_inventory:set_as_inventory_for(player, { title = param })
        end
    end,
})

-- /inv_off removes the form, see below.
core.register_chatcommand("inv_off", {
    description = "Remove the custom inventory form",
    func = function(name)
        local player = core.get_player_by_name(name)
        if player then
            example_inventory:unset_as_inventory_for(player)
        end
    end,
})

Open your inventory and click the button: the counter goes up, and the form is redrawn with the new context.

Like with the show_hud function (see HUDs), update* functions don't do anything, so to update it, call example_inventory:set_as_inventory_for(player, new_ctx) again with the new context. If the context is not provided, it will reuse the existing context of the same form. This is different from HUDs, which never keep a context. Passing a new context replaces the existing one, so values that were stored in the old one are gone. See Context Lifetime by Mode.

The /inv_title chat command above does this. Keep your inventory open while you run it and the title changes straight away. The command passes a new context, which replaces the old one, so the click counter goes back to 0.

If the player has the inventory open when you do this, it is redrawn straight away: Luanti compares the new formspec with the one on screen and rebuilds the screen if they differ. As with any redraw, text that the player has typed into a field but not yet sent is lost. If the new formspec is identical to the old one, nothing is sent.

Flow does the same when the player does something in the inventory that needs a redraw (an on_event function returning true, for example). Other changes to ctx.form that do not need a redraw are applied when the player closes the inventory, so they show up the next time it is opened.

While the form will of course be cleared when the player leaves, if you'd like to unset the inventory manually, call example_inventory:unset_as_inventory_for(player), analogue to close_hud (see HUDs).

For example, after the /inv_off chat command above, the inventory key shows the default inventory (or nothing, depending on your game) instead of the form.

This will set the inventory formspec string to "" and stop flow from processing inventory formspec input.

docs.title: Layout Elements
docs.text:
You should do local gui = flow.widgets in your code to improve readability. All examples will assume that this line exists.

These elements control how other elements are arranged. Most of them draw nothing themselves: they place the elements inside them, work out how big everything is, and share out any spare space. Elements that draw something or accept input (labels, buttons, fields, ...) are described in Functional Elements. To place elements at exact coordinates instead, see Manual Positioning.

Warning: Do not use w and h to size gui.VBox, gui.HBox, or gui.Stack, use min_w and min_h instead: these elements always work out their size from their contents. The one exception is manual positioning with a gui.Stack: if you set both w and h, flow does not position its children, so each child keeps its own x and y and needs its own w and h (see the noclip example). Setting only one of them makes flow overwrite the children's x and y. See Common Aspects for which elements take w and h.

docs.title: gui.VBox
docs.text:
A vertical box, similar to a VBox in GTK. Elements inside a VBox are stacked vertically.

gui.VBox {
    gui.Label { label = "I am a label!" },

    -- Positioned underneath the first one.
    gui.Label { label = "I am a second label!" },
}

Elements inside boxes have a spacing of 0.2 between them. Add spacing = <number> to change it (gui.HBox and gui.Flow work the same way). Spacing is the gap between elements, while padding is the space around one element.

docs.title: gui.HBox
docs.text:
Like gui.VBox but stacks elements horizontally instead.

gui.HBox {
    gui.Label { label = "I am a label!" },

    -- Positioned to the right of the first one.
    gui.Label { label = "I am a second label!" },

    -- You can nest HBox and VBox elements
    gui.VBox {
        gui.Image { w = 1, h = 1, texture_name = "default_dirt.png", align_h = "center" },
        gui.Label { label = "Dirt", expand = true, align_h = "center" },
    }
}

docs.title: gui.ScrollableVBox
docs.text:
Similar to gui.VBox, but shows its contents in an area of a fixed size that the player can scroll, and automatically adds a scrollbar next to it. Anything outside the area is hidden until it is scrolled into view. The area is w by h, both are optional: the width defaults to the width of the contents and the height defaults to the height of the contents, up to a maximum of 5.

On clients too old to support scrolling areas (before Luanti 5.4), flow shows one page of the contents at a time instead, with < and > buttons to change page.

To change how the scrollbar looks, set custom_scrollbar to a table of parameters for gui.Scrollbar, for example custom_scrollbar = {w = 0.8} to make it wider.

gui.ScrollableVBox {
    -- Required. It keeps flow from mixing up scrollbar states if
    -- elements are removed or reordered.
    name = "vbox1",

    -- Optional, defaults to min(height_of_content, 5). This is shorter
    -- than the contents, so a scrollbar is added.
    h = 2,

    gui.Label { label = "I am a label!" },
    gui.Label { label = "I am a second label!" },

    -- The rest is hidden until the player scrolls down.
    gui.Label { label = "I am a third label!" },
    gui.Label { label = "I am a fourth label!" },
}

docs.title: gui.Spacer
docs.text:
A "flexible space" element that expands by default. A spacer only fills spare room, so this box has a min_w and a background color to show how much there is:

gui.HBox {
    min_w = 12,
    bgcolor = "#335577", -- Only here to show the edges of the box.

    -- On the left-hand side
    gui.Button { label = "Cancel" },
    gui.Button { label = "< Back" },

    gui.Spacer {},

    -- On the right-hand side
    gui.Button { label = "Next >" },
    gui.Button { label = "Confirm" },
}

Prefer expand = true with align_h or align_v when that gives the same result. Spacers are implemented as hidden containers, so a few things behave differently from other elements:

  • A spacer counts as an element when flow adds the spacing between the elements of a box. Each spacer therefore adds a gap on each side of it, which is taken out of the spare room it fills. If the box has no spare room, the spacer has no width but the gaps are still there.
  • A spacer cannot have child elements and flow raises an error if you give it any.
  • Several spacers (or other elements with expand = true) in the same box share the spare space equally.

For a spacer, "auto" alignment means "fill" (see Automatic Alignment).

You can get the same layout without a spacer: the expand = true button takes the spare space and align_h = "left" keeps it at its normal width.

gui.HBox {
    min_w = 12,
    bgcolor = "#335577",

    gui.Button { label = "Cancel" },
    gui.Button { label = "< Back", expand = true, align_h = "left" },
    gui.Button { label = "Next >" },
    gui.Button { label = "Confirm" },
}

Do not use spacers to center elements. It creates unnecessary boxes, and labels may end up slightly off-center, because label widths depend on screen size and DPI and this code does not trigger the centering hack. The centering hack is what flow does when align_h or expand centers or stretches a label: it draws the label as a background-less button as wide as the whole area, so the client centers the text itself.

-- This is bad!
gui.HBox {
    min_w = 12,
    bgcolor = "#335577",

    gui.Spacer {},
    gui.Label { label = "I am not properly centered!" },
    gui.Spacer {},
}

Do this instead:

gui.VBox {
    min_w = 12,
    bgcolor = "#335577",

    gui.Label { label = "I am centered!", align_h = "center" },
}

docs.title: gui.Nil
docs.text:
A tool for ternary-ish conditional elements. Unlike visible = false (see Hiding Elements), which keeps its space, a gui.Nil takes up none. Untick the checkbox to remove the box: the last label moves up.

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Checkbox { name = "show_box", label = "Show the box", selected = true },
        gui.Label { label = "The box below is only present if the box is ticked:" },
        ctx.form.show_box ~= false and gui.Box { w = 1, h = 1, color = "#FF0000" }
            or gui.Nil {},
        gui.Label { label = "I move up when the box disappears." },
    }
end)

Use sparingly: flow still has to process each Nil to remove it.

docs.title: gui.Container
docs.text: A group of elements that you position yourself with x and y instead of letting flow lay them out. See Manual Positioning.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Container {
    w = 6, h = 2, -- Optional
    { type = "box", x = 0, y = 0, w = 1, h = 1, color = "red" },
    { type = "label", x = 1, y = 1.5, label = "Hello world!" },
}

docs.title: gui.Stack
docs.text:
This container element places its children on top of each other. All child elements are expanded in both directions.

Note that some elements (such as centred labels) won't pass clicks through to the element below them.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Stack {
    min_w = 10,
    gui.Button { label = "Hello world!" },

    -- A red square, drawn on top of the button. The texture is made with a
    -- texture modifier, so this example does not need any files.
    gui.Image { w = 1, h = 1, texture_name = "[fill:16x16:red", padding = 0.2, align_h = "left" },
}

docs.title: gui.PaginatedVBox
docs.text:
Like gui.ScrollableVBox, but splits the contents into pages instead of scrolling. Only one page is shown at a time, with a < button, a "Page 1 of 3" label, and a > button underneath to change page. It needs a unique name, and w and h work the same way as for gui.ScrollableVBox. Elements are never cut in half: an element that does not fit on a page starts the next one.

gui.ScrollableVBox uses this automatically on clients that cannot scroll.

docs.title: gui.Flow
docs.text: A container with a fixed width that wraps its children onto new rows when they do not fit. You must give it a w, and it does not support h, min_w, or padding. Use spacing to change the gap between elements (the default is the same as for gui.VBox). See Experimental Features for details and an example.

docs.title: gui.Padding (Deprecated)
docs.text: Wraps a single element to add padding around it. It is deprecated and logs a warning, use the padding parameter of the element itself instead, see Padding.

docs.title: Dynamic Element Types
docs.text:
A gui.Label{...} call just returns a table with type = "label" added to it, so you can write {type = "label", label = "Hello world!"} instead of gui.Label{label="Hello world!"}. This is what you need inside gui.Container (see below), and it is also useful if you want to choose the element type from a variable. The type is the name of the gui function in lowercase with underscores between words, for example "item_image_button" for gui.ItemImageButton. The element types table in Styling lists many of them.

HBoxes and VBoxes can be created this way as well (with type = "hbox" and type = "vbox") and work anywhere gui.HBox and gui.VBox do. However, gui.ScrollableVBox, gui.PaginatedVBox, gui.Spacer, gui.Flow, and gui.Nil are functions that build other elements instead of element types, so they cannot be created with a type table. The flow mod does not recognize those type names, and showing the form fails with an Unknown element error.

An example of this is in example.lua in the flow repository.

docs.title: Manual Positioning of Elements
docs.text: You can use gui.Container elements to contain manually positioned elements. Every element inside a container has an x and y, which is the distance of its top-left corner from the top-left corner of the container, in the same units as w and h. Containers can be nested, in which case the offsets add up. If you do not give a w and h, flow uses the smallest size that fits all the elements inside.

docs.title: Container Example
docs.text:
gui.VBox {
    gui.Label { label = "Automatically positioned" },

    -- The container is placed below the label by the VBox, and the
    -- elements inside it are placed at their own x and y.
    gui.Container {
        { type = "box", x = 0, y = 0, w = 1, h = 1, color = "red" },
        { type = "box", x = 0.3, y = 0.3, w = 1, h = 1, color = "green" },
        { type = "box", x = 0.6, y = 0.6, w = 1, h = 1, color = "blue" },
        { type = "label", x = 2, y = 1.1, label = "Manually positioned" }
    },
}

docs.title: Container: noclip Example
docs.text:
Luanti cuts off elements that stick out of the form unless their noclip style is true. This example puts a button and a box outside a 2 by 2 area, which is why it needs noclip. The gui.Stack is only a reference area: it draws nothing, and gives the two containers a known size to be placed against. Setting both w and h on a gui.Stack is supported for this: flow does not lay out such a stack, so its children keep their own x and y. In every other case flow positions the children itself and overwrites their x and y, which is why a stack with only w, or with min_w and min_h, would lose the x = -1 of the second container. See the warning in Layout Elements.

gui.Stack {
    -- With both w and h set, flow does not position the stack's
    -- children, so each keeps its own x and y. Each child then needs its
    -- own x, y, w, and h. With only one of w and h set, flow positions
    -- the children and discards their x and y.
    w = 2, h = 2,
    padding = 0,

    gui.Container {
        -- A container with no size takes no room, so it only marks a
        -- point.
        w = 0, h = 0,
        x = 0, y = 0,

        -- This moves the container itself: its top-left corner goes to
        -- the middle of the stack (x = 1). It does not move or center
        -- the elements inside it.
        align_h = "center",

        -- Elements inside a container are placed by their top-left corner,
        -- relative to the container. The button is 1 by 1 and ends up at
        -- x = 1, y = -1: directly above the right half of the stack.
        {
            type = "button", padding = 0,
            x = 0, y = -1, w = 1, h = 1,
            label = "☺",
            style = {
                noclip = true,
                font_size = "*3",
            },
        },
    },

    -- These x-offsets cancel each other out.
    gui.Container {
        w = 0, h = 0,
        x = -1, y = 0,

        -- "start" leaves the container where it is. Alignment applies to
        -- the container, never to the elements inside it.
        align_h = "start",

        -- The container is at x = -1 and the box is 1 to the right of it,
        -- so the box ends up at x = 0, y = -2: above the left edge of the
        -- stack.
        {
            type = "box", x = 1, y = -2, w = 1, h = 1,
            color = "green", style = { noclip = true },
        },
    },
}

noclip is a style of each element, and the style of an element only applies to that element, so set it on every element that sticks out, as both of the elements above do.

A container can also go inside a gui.Stack, see gui.Stack.

Do not put layout elements (like gui.VBox, gui.HBox, and gui.Stack) inside gui.Container, whether you write them with gui.VBox or with type = "vbox". A container never lays out its children, it only places them at their x and y. If you need a box inside a container anyway, this table shows what happens:

Container has w and h Box has w and h Result No No Works: flow lays out the box. padding, align_h, and align_v on the box are not applied. No Yes Broken: the box's children get no positions. Yes No Broken: flow stops with an error. Yes Yes Broken: the box's children get no positions.

This does not stop you from using a gui.Container inside a layouting element, as in the example above. To get the same effect inside a container, put the elements at exact x and y positions yourself.

docs.title: Unsupported Features
docs.text: Flow does not support everything that Luanti formspecs can do. This page lists what is missing, so you know before you look for it. Where there is a way to get a similar result, it is mentioned. Each formspec element links to its description in the Luanti API documentation.

docs.title: Missing Elements
docs.text: Formspec element What it does What to do instead hypertip[] A tooltip that shows formatted text (see Hypertext Markup). Flow tooltips only show plain text with the tooltip parameter or gui.Tooltip. The markup language can only be used in gui.Hypertext. allow_close[] Stops the Escape key (and similar) from closing the form. Nothing. Players can always close a flow form. You can run code when they do with on_quit, but you cannot stop it. listimages[] Pictures for the background of inventory slots. gui.Listcolors only sets colors. label[x,y;w,h;text] A label that wraps long text inside a given size (an "area label"). gui.Textarea without a name, or gui.Hypertext. Because of this, the halign and valign styles do not do anything for gui.Label. tooltip[x,y;w,h;...] A tooltip for an area instead of an element. The tooltip parameter of any element (flow uses the area of an element without a name for you). gui.Tooltip can only be attached to a named element. field[name;label;default] A small form with a single field and an automatic "Proceed" button (for example for signs). Use a gui.Field and a gui.Button.

docs.title: Missing Parameters
docs.text:
• Content padding of scroll containers. Luanti can work out the range of a scroll container's scrollbar for you, but flow's gui.ScrollContainer does not expose this, so you have to set the range yourself with gui.ScrollbarOptions. gui.ScrollableVBox already does this for you.
  • Node formspec inventory locations. The "current_node" inventory location refers to the node whose formspec is open. A flow form cannot be the formspec of a node, so use "nodemeta:X,Y,Z" to show a node's inventory instead.

docs.title: Things Flow Does for You
docs.text:
These formspec elements exist, but flow generates them itself and you cannot write them:

  • size[]: The size of the form is worked out from the elements in it.
  • position[], anchor[], and padding[]: Use the window_position, window_anchor, and window_padding options of the root element, see Window Position.
  • no_prepend[] and bgcolor[]: Use the no_prepend option and the bgcolor, fbgcolor, and bg_fullscreen options of the root element.
  • real_coordinates[]: Flow always uses the newer coordinate system, where there is no hidden padding or spacing between elements.
  • container_end[] and scroll_container_end[]: Elements inside gui.Container and gui.ScrollContainer are written inside the table.
  • formspec_version[]: Flow always uses formspec version 7.

docs.title: Newer Luanti Features
docs.text:
Because flow always uses formspec version 7 (Luanti 5.8), features that were added in newer versions may not work, even if the missing element or parameter is not listed above. This includes the area label (version 9), floating-point animation frames in gui.Model (version 10), and the halign and valign styles of fields and text areas (version 11), and the editable style of checkboxes, dropdowns, and fields (version 12, the only addition in that version). Formspec versions are described in the "Formspec Version History" section of the Luanti API documentation.

Flow does not check the formspec version when it writes style properties. A property such as halign, valign, or editable is put in the style[] or style_type[] element exactly as you gave it, and is not removed or changed.

The version that flow declares (7) does not stop a newer feature from working. In the current Luanti client source, the client does not compare the form's version with the version a feature was added in. It only asks whether the client itself knows the feature. So halign and valign work for players on Luanti 5.17 or newer, editable works on Luanti 5.18 or newer, and the area label (an extra parameter of label[]) is accepted by clients that know it, all from a form that says version 7.

What happens on a client that is too old depends on the feature. In the current source, a style property that the client does not know is skipped and the other properties of the same style[] still apply. An element with more parameters than the client knows is not drawn at all, and the client logs an error. Clients older than the current source were not checked.

docs.title: Formspec Versions and Luanti Releases
docs.text: Formspec version Luanti release Notable additions 2 5.1.0 Real coordinates always on, background9[] 3 5.2.0 Draw order follows definition order, scroll_container[] 4 5.4.0 Dropdown index events 5 5.5.0 padding[] 6 5.6.0 Nine-slice images, animated_image[] 7 5.8.0 Focused button state, field_enter_after_edit[] (the version flow uses) 8 5.10.0 Scroll container content padding 9 5.12.0 allow_close[], area label[] 10 5.13.0 Floating-point model[] frames 11 5.17.0 hypertip[], text alignment styles 12 5.18.0 editable style

docs.title: Scrollbar Textures Do Not Work
docs.text:
scrollbar_bg, slider, arrow_up, and arrow_down should not be used. Flow accepts them, but Luanti has no such parameters, and on Luanti 5.8 and newer a scrollbar that sets any of them is not shown at all.

Flow (through formspec_ast) writes the four textures as one comma-separated sixth parameter after value, leaving the ones you did not set empty. Luanti's scrollbar[] takes exactly five parameters. It only tolerates extra parameters when the form's formspec version is newer than the highest version the client supports, and flow always uses version 7:

Luanti version Highest formspec version Result 5.6 and 5.7 6 The extra parameter is ignored and the scrollbar is shown with its normal look. 5.8 and newer 7 or higher The scrollbar is rejected and not shown, and an error is logged.

The rejection was confirmed in-game with a gui.Scrollbar that set all four textures and one that set only slider. A scrollbar without textures next to them was shown normally.

Sources (Luanti source code):

  • GUIFormSpecMenu::parseScrollBar requires between 5 and 5 parameters, and nothing in guiFormSpecMenu.cpp reads the textures: 5.8.0, 5.7.0, master.
  • GUIFormSpecMenu::precheckElement in the same file accepts extra parameters only when m_formspec_version > FORMSPEC_API_VERSION, and otherwise logs Invalid <element> element(<count>) and skips the element.
  • FORMSPEC_API_VERSION is 6 in 5.7.0, 7 in 5.8.0, and 12 in master.
  • The formspec documentation lists scrollbar[] with five parameters: position, size, orientation, name, and value.

docs.title: Padding, Spacing, and Backgrounds
docs.text:
Most elements can have a padding value, which will add the specified amount of padding around the element, measured in slot units. The "root" element of the form (the one returned by the build function) has a default padding of 0.3, everything else has a default padding of 0.

padding is ignored on these elements:

  • gui.Flow, gui.ScrollableVBox, and gui.PaginatedVBox. To pad one, put it inside a gui.VBox (or another layouting element) and set padding on that instead.
  • Elements inside a gui.Container, which are placed at their x and y and are not padded.
  • Invisible elements such as gui.Style, which take up no space.

There is also a deprecated gui.Padding element that wraps a single element and pads it. Use the padding parameter instead.

HBox and VBox have a spacing field which specifies how much spacing there is between elements inside the box. Its default value is described in gui.VBox.

Box elements (gui.HBox and gui.VBox) can optionally have bgimg and bgimg_middle parameters that specify a background for the box. bgimg is the name of a texture, which is stretched to fill the box. If bgimg_middle is set as well, the texture is drawn as a nine-slice whose corners are bgimg_middle pixels big, so one small texture can make a background of any size. The background will be drawn behind any padding that the box has.

The examples below use a small 16x16 texture, a white border around a blue square. It is made with texture modifiers, so no file is needed. Because the border is only 2 pixels wide, you can see how it is stretched.

Example with only bgimg. The whole texture is stretched, so the border gets thick and blurry:

gui.VBox {
    -- Stretch the texture over the whole box
    bgimg = "[fill:16x16:white^[fill:12x12:2,2:#336699",

    gui.Button { label = "Button 1" },
    gui.Button { label = "Button 2" },
}

Example with bgimg_middle as well. The corners and edges keep their 2 pixel border, and only the middle is stretched:

gui.VBox {
    padding = 0.5,
    spacing = 0.1,

    -- Draw the texture as a nine-slice
    bgimg = "[fill:16x16:white^[fill:12x12:2,2:#336699",
    bgimg_middle = 2,

    gui.Button { label = "Button 1" },
    gui.Button { label = "Button 2" },
}

The padding around the VBox is 0.5 and the spacing between the buttons inside it is 0.1.

docs.title: Popovers (Highly Experimental)
docs.text:
This API will likely have breaking changes in the future.

Flow supports a highly experimental low-level API for defining popovers. Popovers appear over top of all other elements and are anchored to their parent.

This API is intended to be used for creating themed elements like dropdowns, or for a higher level popover API that adds styling and is easier to use.

You add a popover attribute to any container element to define a popover. Flow does not manage the lifecycle (opening/closing) of popovers, you must ensure that you do this yourself like in the example.

Two parameters go on the container that owns the popover:

  • popover: the element to show over the container, or nil for no popover.
  • on_close_popover: a function that flow calls with (player, ctx) when the player clicks anywhere outside the popover. Like an on_event function, it can return true to redraw the form. Flow only adds this click catcher while a popover is shown.

Here is the smallest useful popover: a button that opens a popover with one label, and on_close_popover to close it again. The popover is only given to the container while ctx.show_popover is set, and is nil otherwise (cond and element or nil is the usual Lua way to write that):

local gui = flow.widgets

local my_gui = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        -- Leave room around the button so the popover stays inside the form.
        padding = 3,

        gui.Stack {
            gui.Button {
                label = "Open popover",
                on_event = function(player, ctx)
                    ctx.show_popover = true
                    return true
                end,
            },

            popover = ctx.show_popover and gui.VBox {
                padding = 0.2,
                bgcolor = "#222e",
                gui.Label { label = "Hi there!" },
            } or nil,

            -- Called when the player clicks outside the popover.
            on_close_popover = function(player, ctx)
                ctx.show_popover = false
                return true
            end,
        },
    }
end)

docs.title: Where the Popover Goes
docs.text:
side decides which edge of the container the popover is attached to: "bottom" (the default, also used for any other value), "top", "left", or "right". The popover is then lined up along that edge with align_h for "top" and "bottom", or align_v for "left" and "right" (the other one is ignored). The alignment is relative to the container, not to the form:

Alignment Result "start" The popover's left (or top) edge lines up with the container's. "end" The popover's right (or bottom) edge lines up with the container's. "center" The popover is centered on the container. "fill", or unset The popover is stretched to the width (or height) of the container.

The full example below puts side in a dropdown inside the popover, so that you can try every side. side = ctx.form.side is nil on the first draw, which means "bottom", and the dropdown stores its choice in ctx.form.side. Elements inside a popover that are not named keys (such as the label and the dropdown) are its children, in the same table as the named keys.

The popover is drawn from the build function, so it can depend on ctx:

local gui = flow.widgets

local my_gui = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        -- Some padding is added for the purposes of the demo so that the popup
        -- isn't off-screen
        padding = 3,
        gui.Label { label = "Popover demo:" },

        gui.Stack {
            gui.Button {
                label = "Open popover",

                -- When the popover button is clicked, open the popover
                on_event = function(player, ctx)
                    ctx.show_popover = true
                    return true
                end,
            },

            -- The actual element to overlay
            -- "popover" is set to the gui.VBox element if (and only if)
            -- ctx.show_popover is true, otherwise it's nil so no popover is
            -- shown.
            popover = ctx.show_popover and gui.VBox {
                -- Specifying padding and bgcolor is optional, but is probably
                -- a good idea since flow doesn't do any styling on its own.
                padding = 0.2,
                bgcolor = "#222e",

                -- "side" specifies how the popover is positioned relative to
                -- the parent, and can be "bottom" (default), "top", "left", or
                -- "right". It is nil on the first draw, which means "bottom".
                side = ctx.form.side,

                -- align_h and align_v align the popover according to its
                -- parent element. You only need to specify align_h for
                -- side = "top"/"bottom" or align_v for side = "left"/"right",
                -- this example specifies both so that it can demonstrate
                -- switching between different sides.
                align_h = "fill",
                align_v = "center",

                -- Popover contents
                gui.Label { label = "Hi there!" },
                gui.Dropdown {
                    name = "side",
                    items = {
                        "bottom",
                        "top",
                        "left",
                        "right",
                    },
                },
            } or nil,

            -- Clicking outside the popover will call this function, which
            -- should probably close the popover.
            on_close_popover = function(player, ctx)
                ctx.show_popover = false
                return true
            end,
        },

        gui.Label { label = "After popover button" },
    }
end)

Show the form with my_gui:show(player) as usual.

align_h and align_v are among the parameters shared by all elements.

There are some restrictions on popovers:

  • They must not extend outside the form, otherwise they'll only be partially visible (unless everything is styled with noclip = true). Flow does not attempt to detect this.
  • You can only define popover on container elements, like gui.Stack, gui.HBox, and gui.VBox.
  • Only one popover is shown at a time.
  • Players can still use tab to interact with things behind the popover, despite being unable to use their mouse to do so.
  • You cannot show popovers inside of other popovers.
  • Popovers cannot be on the root element.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: A player's client can send anything to the server. A normal client only sends values that the form could produce, but a modified one can send other names, other values, and several actions at once. This page lists what flow checks before it stores a value or calls one of your functions, and what it leaves to you.

docs.title: What Flow Checks
docs.text:
• The form. Flow only handles input for the form that the player has open right now. Every time a form is shown with form:show() it gets a new internal name, so input that is meant for an old or made-up form is ignored.
  • The elements. Flow only stores values for named inputs that were in the form it drew, and only calls on_event and on_key_enter functions of elements that were in it. Anything else the client sends is ignored. Hidden elements are not part of the form, see Hiding Elements.
  • Size. A value longer than 60,000 bytes is ignored and a warning is logged.
  • Text. Control characters other than tabs and newlines are removed from the text of gui.Field, gui.Pwdfield, and gui.Textarea, and from the value of a gui.Hypertext action. The same goes for the control characters from U+0080 to U+009F. Newlines are also removed from gui.Field, where a player can only enter one by pasting it.
  • Checkboxes. The value is always true or false.
  • Dropdowns. The value must be one of the items. With index_event = true it must be a number from 1 to the number of items. On clients that support it, flow always asks for the item number instead of the text, so the client never gets to choose the text.
  • Tabs, tables, and text lists. The selected tab or row must be a number from 1 to the number of tabs or rows. Decimals are rounded down.
  • Buttons. Flow calls the on_event function of at most one button per submission, and not at the same time as an on_key_enter function. Buttons never store a value.

When a value is rejected, ctx.form keeps its previous value. The other values in the same submission are still used.

docs.title: What You Still Need to Check
docs.text:
• Who is allowed to do something. Flow can tell that a button exists in the form, but not whether the player really clicked it. A modified client can trigger the on_event function of any element that is currently in the form. Check privileges, ownership, distances and so on inside the function, the same as you would in a chat command.
  • What is in the value. Flow does not limit text to a length (apart from 60,000 bytes), and it does not check scrollbar positions against the range of the scrollbar. Check values that matter before you use them, for example before putting text into a node's metadata.
  • Inventories. The slots of a gui.List are handled by Luanti, flow does not check or limit what is moved. Use the inventory callbacks that Luanti provides.
  • Hypertext. Flow does not look at the markup that you give gui.Hypertext, see Hypertext Markup. Escape text from players with core.hypertext_escape().

Everything in ctx except ctx.form is only changed by your code, so the client cannot change it.

docs.title: Text in Elements
docs.text: Text that you put in an element, such as a label, is escaped when flow generates the formspec, so it cannot add or change other elements.

docs.title: Styling Forms
docs.text:
Styles change how elements look: their colors, images, fonts, and so on. A style is a set of properties such as bgcolor = "red", and which properties exist depends on the type of element. All of them are listed in the property reference below.

You can style a single element with the style field (the inline syntax), or style many elements at once with the gui.Style and gui.StyleType elements (see separate style elements).

Which one to use:

You want to Use Style one element, or a few that share a table The inline style field Style one element by its name, or support old versions of flow gui.Style Style every element of a type (every button, say) after this point gui.StyleType Change the size of an element (font_size, list size and spacing) The inline style field only, see Styles That Change Size

docs.title: Inline Syntax
docs.text:
Inline styles were added in May 2024, so older versions of flow do not support this syntax, and the sub-style syntax (the sel entries) may change in the future. Only use inline styles for things that are not essential, so that your form does not look broken without them, or use separate style elements if you need to support older versions.

You can add inline styles to elements with the style field:

gui.Button {
    label = "Test",
    style = {
        bgcolor = "red",

        -- You can style specific states of elements:
        { sel = "$hovered", bgcolor = "green" },

        -- Or a combination of states:
        { sel = "$hovered, $pressed", bgcolor = "blue" },
        { sel = "$hovered+pressed", bgcolor = "white" },
    },
}

Properties directly inside style always apply. A sel entry only applies in the listed states, and $ stands for the element itself (so "$hovered+pressed" is "button:hovered+pressed" for an unnamed button). Separate states with a comma to match any of them, or join them with + to require all of them. Every comma-separated entry needs its own $, or it is skipped with a logged warning.

If you need to style multiple elements, you can reuse the style table:

local my_style = { bgcolor = "red", { sel = "$hovered", bgcolor = "green" } }

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Button { label = "Styled button", style = my_style },
        gui.Button { label = "Unstyled button" },
        gui.Button { label = "Second styled button", style = my_style },
    }
end)

Styling an unnamed element can undo other styles

Luanti can only style unnamed elements by their type, so flow applies the style to every element of that type and then resets those properties to their defaults straight after the element. This also undoes any earlier gui.StyleType for the same properties, for every element of that type that comes after. Give the element a name to avoid this.

In this form, button A is blue because of the gui.StyleType, button B is red, and button C is not blue: the style on B reset bgcolor for every button after it. Button D has a name, so its style is applied to it alone and nothing is reset:

gui.VBox {
    gui.StyleType { selectors = { "button" }, props = { bgcolor = "blue" } },

    gui.Button { label = "A" },
    gui.Button { label = "B", style = { bgcolor = "red" } },
    gui.Button { label = "C" },
    gui.Button { name = "d", label = "D", style = { bgcolor = "red" } },
}

Property values are normally strings, but flow also accepts numbers and booleans where a property needs one. Setting a property to an empty string (bgimg = "") resets it to its default value.

docs.title: Separate Style Elements
docs.text:
Alternatively, use the gui.Style and gui.StyleType elements to style a large group of elements or to support older versions of flow:

gui.VBox {
    gui.Style { selectors = { "btn1" }, props = { bgcolor = "red", border = false } },

    gui.Button { name = "btn1", label = "Styled by name" },
    gui.Button { name = "btn2", label = "Not styled" },
}

The Style and StyleType elements are invisible and won't affect padding. They only affect the elements that come after them, so put them before the elements you want to style.

docs.title: Styles That Change Size
docs.text:
Flow works out the size of an element before it writes any styles, so it has to see a style that changes the size. It only does that in some cases:

  • gui.Style and gui.StyleType do not support styles that change the element size. Flow only sees these properties in the inline syntax, so use that for them.
  • font_size changes the size of gui.Labels, buttons, and the default text of fields only if it starts with * (such as "*2") and is set with the inline syntax. Other values still change the text but not the size of the element.
  • The labels above fields and checkboxes ignore font_size, and a gui.Label with a fixed h is positioned as if font_size was not set. That behavior is deprecated and flow logs a warning when it detects it, so leave h out of labels that use font_size.
  • The size and spacing styles of gui.List (added in March 2025) count too, but only whole numbers such as "2,2" or "0,0" and only in the inline syntax.

docs.title: Selectors and States
docs.text:
selectors is a list that says which elements the style applies to:

  • gui.Style selects elements by their name, so {"btn1"} styles the element with name = "btn1".
  • gui.StyleType selects elements by their type, so {"button"} styles every button that comes after it. The type is the element's name in lowercase with underscores between words, for example item_image_button for gui.ItemImageButton. Some types also style other types, see element types.
  • gui.StyleType also accepts "*", which selects every element.

A selector can end with a colon and one or more states to only style the element while it is in that state, such as "btn1:hovered" or "button:hovered+pressed" (+ means all of the states have to be active).

In this form, the text turns yellow on every button, and a button turns blue while the mouse is over it. The label is not a button, so it is not affected:

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.StyleType {
            selectors = { "button", "image_button" },
            props = { textcolor = "yellow" },
        },
        gui.StyleType {
            selectors = { "button:hovered" },
            props = { bgcolor = "#336699" },
        },

        gui.Button { label = "Hover over me" },
        gui.Button { label = "Me too" },
        gui.Label { label = "I am not a button." },
    }
end)

docs.title: States
docs.text:
Every element has the default state, which is the same as not giving any state. Buttons (gui.Button, gui.ButtonExit, gui.ImageButton, gui.ItemImageButton) also have these states:

State Active when focused The button has keyboard focus hovered The mouse is over the button pressed The button is being pressed

docs.title: Element Types
docs.text:
These are the types that can be styled. A type that "inherits" from another also uses the styles set for the other type, for example a style set on image also applies to animated_image.

Type Element Inherits from animated_image gui.AnimatedImage image box gui.Box button gui.Button button_url gui.ButtonURL Not valid, style by name button_exit gui.ButtonExit button checkbox gui.Checkbox dropdown gui.Dropdown field gui.Field image gui.Image image_button gui.ImageButton image_button_exit gui.ImageButtonExit Not valid, style by name item_image gui.ItemImage Only supports noclip item_image_button gui.ItemImageButton label gui.Label list gui.List model gui.Model pwdfield gui.Pwdfield field scrollbar gui.Scrollbar tabheader gui.Tabheader table gui.Table textarea gui.Textarea textlist gui.Textlist vertlabel gui.Vertlabel label

Luanti also lists hypertip, but flow has no element for it, see Unsupported Features. The item_image type only supports noclip (see Other Elements). Types marked "Not valid" are not in Luanti's list of types, so a gui.StyleType for them does nothing: give those elements a name and style them with gui.Style or the inline syntax.

docs.title: Property Reference
docs.text: Colors are described in Common Aspects, and textures are image file names. A "2D vector" is written as a string such as "1,2". Properties that only list a type of element are not valid on other elements, and an unknown property is ignored.

docs.title: All Elements
docs.text: Property Description noclip Boolean. Set to true to let the element be drawn outside the area of the form. Default false.

docs.title: Text Properties
docs.text:
These properties change how text looks. font and font_size are valid on buttons, labels, fields, tables, and text lists. textcolor is valid on buttons, labels, fields, and tab headers, but not on tables and text lists. The sections below show which applies where.

Property Description font Font type, a comma-separated list. Use at most one of normal (the default font) and mono (a font where every letter is the same width), and any of bold and italic. For example "mono,bold". If you only give bold or italic, normal is used. Default normal. font_size Text size. "16" sets an absolute size, "+2" and "-2" make the text 2 points larger or smaller than the default, and "*1.5" multiplies the default size by 1.5 (like em in CSS). The default is the size the player has chosen in their settings. textcolor Color of the text. Default white.

Which font_size values change the size of an element is described in Styles That Change Size.

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text:
For gui.Button, gui.ButtonExit, gui.ImageButton, and gui.ItemImageButton. Buttons also support font, font_size, and textcolor.

Property Description alpha Boolean. Whether to draw the transparent parts of bgimg. Default true. bgcolor Color that tints the button. bgimg Texture to use as the background of the button. Default none. bgimg_middle Draws bgimg as a nine-slice. Written as a string in one of the formats "x", "x,y", or "x,y,x2,y2", which have the same meaning as middle_x, middle_y, middle_x2, and middle_y2. Also adds padding around the content of the button. border Boolean. Whether to draw the bevelled button border. Set to false to hide it. Default true. content_offset 2D vector that moves the content (text and image) of the button without resizing the button. padding Space between the edges of the button and its content, as a rectangle written in the same formats as bgimg_middle. This value is relative to bgimg_middle. It is not the same as the padding parameter of elements, which adds space outside the element and is handled by flow, see Padding. sound The name of a sound to play when the button is triggered, such as a sound file name from a mod's sounds folder without the extension. It is played at normal volume and takes no other options.

gui.ImageButton has some more properties for the picture drawn on top of the button:

Property Description fgimg The picture to draw. Default none. The texture_name and pressed_texture_name you give to the element take precedence over this. fgimg_middle Draws fgimg as a nine-slice, like bgimg_middle.

Some older properties still work but are deprecated. Use states instead: bgcolor_hovered, bgcolor_pressed, bgimg_hovered, bgimg_pressed, fgimg_hovered, and fgimg_pressed. They work like bgcolor and bgimg but only apply while the button is hovered or pressed.

docs.title: Fields and Text Areas
docs.text:
For gui.Field, gui.Pwdfield, and gui.Textarea. They also support font, font_size, and textcolor.

Property Description border Boolean. Set to false to hide the background and border of the text box. Default true. halign Horizontal alignment of the text: left (default), center, or right. Needs Luanti 5.17 or newer (formspec version 11), but works even though flow declares version 7. Older clients skip it, see Newer Luanti Features. valign Vertical alignment of the text: top (default), center, or bottom. Needs Luanti 5.17 or newer (formspec version 11), but works even though flow declares version 7. Older clients skip it, see Newer Luanti Features. Only has an effect when all of the text fits inside the element. If the text is too long (and a gui.Textarea gets a scrollbar), it is always aligned to the top so that no text is cut off. It also does not work in gui.Field, but halign does.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
For gui.Label and gui.Vertlabel: font, font_size, and textcolor.

Luanti also has halign and valign for labels, but they only apply to the area label, which flow does not have, so they do nothing here (see Unsupported Features).

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
For gui.List:

Property Description size 2D vector. The size of each slot. Default "1,1". spacing 2D vector. The space between slots. Default "0.25,0.25".

Flow uses these values to work out how big a list is, see Styles That Change Size for what it understands.

docs.title: Boxes
docs.text:
For gui.Box. These properties only take effect when the box has no color of its own. The colors, bordercolors, and borderwidths properties can have one, two, or four values separated by commas (like CSS borders):

  • One value, such as "#FF0": used for all corners or borders.
  • Two values, such as "red,#FFAAFF": for the colors, the top-left and bottom-right corners, then the top-right and bottom-left corners. For the widths, the top and bottom borders, then the left and right borders.
  • Four values, such as "blue,#A0F,green,#FFFA": starting with the top-left corner (or the top border) and going clockwise.
Property Description colors Color of the corners of the box. Default black. bordercolors Color of the borders of the box. Default black. borderwidths Width of the borders in pixels, as a whole number. A negative width puts the border inside the box, a positive width puts it outside the box, and 0 draws no border. Default 0.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
For gui.Model:

Property Description bgcolor Background color of the model area.

docs.title: Read-Only Elements (editable)
docs.text: Luanti 5.18 (formspec version 12) added an editable property for gui.Checkbox, gui.Dropdown, gui.Field, gui.Pwdfield, and gui.Textarea. Setting it to false makes the element read-only (default true). Flow does nothing special for it and writes the property unchanged. The client does not check the form's version for it, so it works for players on Luanti 5.18 or newer even though flow declares version 7, and it may be ignored for other players. Do not rely on it alone to stop changes: also ignore changes to the element in your own code. See also Newer Luanti Features.

docs.title: Other Elements
docs.text: Element Properties gui.Checkbox sound: A sound to play when the box is ticked or unticked. gui.Dropdown sound: A sound to play when a different item is selected. gui.Tabheader sound: A sound to play when a different tab is selected. textcolor: Color of the tab text, default white. gui.Table, gui.Textlist font and font_size. The colors of a table are set with gui.TableOptions. gui.Image, gui.AnimatedImage, gui.ItemImage, gui.Scrollbar Only noclip.

docs.title: Tooltips
docs.text:
A tooltip is a small box of text that appears when the player hovers over an element.

Add a tooltip to an element with the tooltip field. Hover over the elements below to see them:

gui.VBox {
    gui.Button { label = "Hover over me", tooltip = "I am a button tooltip!" },
    gui.Label { label = "Hover over me too", tooltip = "Labels work as well." },
}

This works on elements without a name as well. In that case the tooltip covers the area of the element, and the tooltip of a named element that overlaps it takes priority.

If the areas of two unnamed elements overlap and both have a tooltip (for example in a gui.Stack, or a box with a tooltip that contains an element with its own), the one that comes first in the form wins. Flow puts each tooltip directly before its element, and Luanti shows the first area tooltip that contains the mouse pointer, so the tooltip of a box beats the tooltips of the elements inside it.

There is also a gui.Tooltip element which lets you change the background and text color of the tooltip. It refers to the element it belongs to with gui_element_name, which must be the name of that element, and it should come after that element. As with gui.Style, it is invisible and won't affect padding.

Tooltips are rebuilt every time the form is drawn, so their text can change, see the gui.Tooltip example.

Flow cannot make tooltips that show formatted text (hypertip[]) or tooltips for an arbitrary area instead of an element, see Unsupported Features.
